11304-the-lake:
George Moore's novel The Lake, in this 1921 Heinemann edition, is dedicated in a French epistle to Édouard Dujardin. whose title La Source du Fleuve Chrétien Moore admits borrowing for a character's book. The dedication recalls talks on literature and music at Fontainebleau and Valvins, where Mallarmé lived, and Seine poplars triste in spring. The novel itself concerns an Irish priest, Father Oliver Gogarty, torn between his vocation and a woman's love.

Moore's prose is lyrical and introspective, following conscience rather than action. The Lake is often counted among his finest novels, a study of faith, desire, and escape. Readers of Irish literature will find its quiet intensity distinct from the louder fiction of its era.
12104-ethelyn-s-mistake:
Mary J. Holmes, a best-selling American novelist of the later nineteenth century, wrote Ethelyn Mistake as a domestic romance. The heroine, Ethelyn, marries Richard Markham and must learn to live with his stern mother, his Washington career, and her own quick temper.

Chapters follow the bridal, the honeymoon, housekeeping battles, society calls, long separations, and a crisis that parts husband and wife for years. Letters, investigations, and a slow reconciliation drive the later plot. Holmes writes for readers who liked moral sentiment with their romance, and the book rewards patience: Ethelyn grows from a spoiled girl into a woman who owns her faults. Its picture of middle-class marriage feels dated, but the emotions stay legible.
12731-the-high-school-boys-training-hike:
H. Irving Hancock's High School Boys' Training Hike, or Making Themselves Hard as Nails, follows Dick Prescott and friends on a hike to toughen for football. Chapters run from Mr. Titmouse not knowing Dick and the deed of a hero, a peddler and a lawyer's half, and a no-breakfast plan follow. Making tramps squirm, a frisked peddler, a tame Indian imitation and Reuben Hinman proving his mettle come next.

Tom idealising working clothes, trouble with rah-rah-rahs, a snub, an apple pie and a storm port follow. Home, hospital and almshouse, two kinds of hobo, Dick as knight errant and revenge talk close the book. Hancock writes brisk, moral adventure, where hiking builds character and team. The book is a classic schoolboy tale of grit, humour and fair play.
12823-joe-s-luck-or-always-wide-awake:
Horatio Alger's Joe's Luck, subtitled Always Wide Awake, follows Joe, a stout, sun-browned boy of fifteen who refuses to be ordered about. When Oscar Norton demands that Joe brush him off, Joe answers that he is not Oscar's servant, though Oscar's father employs him. The clash sets Joe on a road of self-reliance.

Later Joe spots a stealthy man with a canvas bag of sand, a weapon that can kill without leaving marks, trailing another traveller. Though only a boy against a ruffian, Joe's courage holds. Alger's moral is plain: stay alert, stand firm, and luck follows work and pluck.
12922-burke:
John Morley's Burke, in the English Men of Letters series, gives a life rather than a critique of Edmund Burke. Morley notes that his earlier Burke study was critical, not narrative, and that only about twenty pages carry over, with three more from his Britannica article. Early life, Ireland, Parliament, and Beaconsfield frame the chapters.

A Bristol passage shows Burke telling merchants he would rather risk displeasing them than injuring them. He refuses to take up or lay down a great system for the convenience of the hour. Morley admires that independence. The book remains a classic short life of a great parliamentary mind.
14664-things-to-make:
A hands-on manual from the early twentieth century sets out projects a keen boy or young maker could build at home or in a small workshop. Its chapters start with plain woodwork. A sawing trestle, a joiner's bench, a bookstand and a house ladder lead to larger jobs, such as a poultry house and a bicycle shed.

Later sections turn to working models and machines. Telegraph gear, a reciprocating electric motor, an electric alarm clock and a model railway sit beside a simple engine, a slide-valve engine, model steam turbines and spinning steam tops. Clear steps and many figures guide each build, while notes warn that steam, electricity and some chemicals need care.
14687-christian-s-mistake:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik's novel opens in Avonsbridge, where Christian Oakley is about to marry the Reverend Arnold Grey, master of Saint Bede's College. Her foster parents draft the newspaper notice with pride, and a snowy December wedding seems to promise a settled, respectable life.

The mistake of the title grows from that bright start. Christian must learn what marriage to a grave, busy clergyman really asks of a young wife, and how love, duty and independence pull against each other. Family, church society and small-town talk shape her choices. Craik tells the story with sympathy for both partners, and with a sharp eye for the gap between a wedding and a life.
16229-the-poems-of-henry-van-dyke:
Henry Van Dyke's Poems, in a new and revised London edition of 1925 from Arthur F. Bird, gathers a lifetime of verse. Printed by the Scribner Press, the volume is dedicated in friendship to Katrina Trask and John Huston Finley. It collects Songs out of Doors, Golden Stars, The Red Flower, and The Grand Canyon. The White Bees, The Builders, Music, and The Toiling of Felix also appear, among others. Earlier books listed run from The Ruling Passion to The Valley of Vision.

Van Dyke's poems move between nature, faith, work, and travel, in clear, musical lines meant to be read aloud. The revised edition adds many pieces never before collected. Readers who like traditional American verse will find a generous, well-ordered single volume.
16330-the-young-priest-s-keepsake:
Michael J. Phelan wrote this keepsake for young priests, above all those bound for foreign missions. Culture comes first, then English, sermon writing, sermon prep, elocution, and the dangers of the hour. A closing chapter sums up the young priest's daily tasks and calls.

Phelan speaks bluntly, as a teacher who has seen good men fail for want of manners, clear speech, or sound English. The second edition of 1909 adds two chapters and runs to a fuller handbook. The book is practical throughout, meant to be kept at hand, not merely read once and shelved.
1655-the-god-of-his-fathers-tales-of-the:
Jack London's God of His Fathers gathers Klondike tales from the 1906 Pitman edition. It opens with the title story. It runs through The Great Interrogation, Siwash, The Man with the Gash, and Jan the Unrepentant, on to Grit of Women, Where the Trail Forks, and At the Rainbow's End.

The tales pit white newcomers against Native peoples, the cold, and their own codes, with London's usual sympathy for endurance and his era's prejudices plain to see. The Scorn of Women closes the set with a bitter note. The book is an early London collection, raw and powerful.
16902-may-brooke:
Mrs. Anna H. Dorsey wrote this 1888 novel May Brooke, subtitled Conscience, or the Trials of May Brooke, issued by P. J. Kenedy in New York and Philadelphia. Chapters move from Uncle Stillinghast and May Brooke into a morning errand and Aunt Mabel. Past and present, Helen, and things of time and eternity follow. Troubled waters, trials, and a warning appear. A midnight messenger, repentance, and a new will lead to a secret sin and a discovery. A death dream, remorse, and a conclusion close the book.

Dorsey tells of a girl caught between a stern uncle, a bad road by the Hazel property, and a cousin's peril, with conscience as her guide. The tale is earnest, Catholic, and moral, in the style of its day. Readers who like old domestic novels will find a heartfelt story of sin, repentance, and a young woman's trials.
17347-sonnets-and-sonnets-on-english-dra:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's sonnets on English dramatic poets, covering 1590 to 1650, appear here as taken from volume five of his collected poetical works. The set honours the playwrights of Shakespeare's age and the decades after, the men who built the English stage in its first great flowering. Swinburne, himself a poet of high passion and musical line, was a natural champion for them.

Each sonnet is a compact tribute, praising a dramatist in fourteen lines of dense, ardent verse. Readers get both an introduction to a crowded stage generation and a sample of Swinburne at his most devoted. The poems reward slow reading, and they show how a Victorian poet claimed the Elizabethan and Jacobean stage as his own inheritance.
17863-blackbeard-or-the-pirate-of-roanok:
B. Barker wrote Blackbeard, or the Pirate of the Roanoke, printed in Boston in 1847 by F. Gleason. Barker, author of The Sea Serpent and The Dwarf of the Channel, here gives a tale of the Atlantic, built round the dread pirate of the Carolina coast.

The tale opens on Trinidad, a small, fair isle in the Atlantic, where the Earl of Derwentwater lands with his party. Strange sounds and enchanted scenes soon give way to the sudden sight of Blackbeard himself. Barker writes in the full, lurid style of the old story papers. It is a rousing pirate yarn, best read for its thrills.
17961-kindness-to-animals-or-the-sin-of-:
The American Sunday-School Union printed Kindness to Animals in Philadelphia in 1845, revised by its committee of publication. The book does not aim to be a natural history; it aims to teach children to be kind to beasts, birds, fishes, and insects they meet each day.

The author tells of creatures he has owned or watched, and he vows to write nothing but what he knows to be true. Chapters move from the start of life to the sin of cruelty, exposed and rebuked. It is a gentle, moral children's book of the 1840s, full of plain tales meant to soften young hearts toward animals.
18126-tales-of-the-chesapeake:
George Alfred Townsend published this 1880 book of pieces about the Chesapeake Bay country. Its scenes center on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, the Pocomoke River, and the small shore towns and inlets where oyster boats worked. Townsend dedicated the book to his father, whose forebears had lived near the Pocomoke for almost two hundred years.

The pieces share one place rather than one plot. They include the stories called Kidnapped and Dominion over the Fish, and a new poem, Herman of Bohemia Manor. Oyster fleets, seine nets, sunset light on old houses, and the sounds of shore work give the book its texture. A reader comes away with a clear picture of bay life in the late nineteenth century.
18671-never-fail-blake:
Arthur Stringer published this mystery novel at New York in 1913, in a series called Supertales of Modern Mystery. Its hero, Blake, second deputy commissioner, is a heavy, gloomy man with hound's eyes. The book opens when a woman named Elsie, calm, beautiful, and known as a lawbreaker, walks into his office at his summons. Their talk sets a cat-and-mouse game in motion.

Stringer builds the tale on Blake's dogged pursuit and Elsie's cool power, with city crime and police work at the fore. The printed book keeps two chapters numbered five, marked five-a and five-b, rather than renumbering the rest. Readers of early detective fiction will find a brisk, atmospheric example.
18743-krindlesyke:
Wilfrid Gibson's verse drama Krindlesyke, published by Macmillan of London in 1922, takes its name from a remote shepherd's cottage on the Northumbrian fells. The cottage stands at least three miles from any other dwelling, a bleak stone block of two rooms, a but and a ben.

Book One, first drafted for an obscure stage showing in 1910 and wholly rewritten since, centers on Phoebe Barrasford. Her father Ezra, an old herd blinded by hot tar, sits by the door while her mother Eliza makes griddle-cakes over peat, awaiting the return of Jim, away to wed. Gibson flavors the verse with local words of feeling rather than strict dialect, letting the sense carry even for south-country readers.
18934-my-lady-nicotine-a-study-in-smoke:
J. M. Barrie, author of Sentimental Tommy, published this humorous study of smoking, illustrated by M. B. Prendergast, with Knight and Millet in Boston. Its chapters compare matrimony and smoking, recall a first cigar, praise the Arcadia mixture, and describe pipes, pouch, and smoking-table. Friends named Gilray, Marriot, Jimmy, and Scrymgeour share the smoke.

Barrie writes with affection for the rituals of the pipe: the house-boat Arcadia, the romance of a pipe-cleaner, how heroes smoke, and the ghost of Christmas Eve. The tone is playful, even as wives' cigars and flowers in pots cause trouble. Readers get a light, witty book by the future creator of Peter Pan, charming for its company of smokers and its praise of small pleasures.
18943-tom-slade-at-black-lake:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh published this Boy Scout novel in 1920, with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Its hero, Tom Slade, is by now a grown man, and Fitzhugh answers readers who asked when Tom would ever grow up: once a Scout, he writes, always a Scout. The story is set around Black Lake, where Tom puts scout craft to work on land and water.

Hauling logs with block and tackle, camping, and helping others in trouble fill the book's action. The emphasis falls on skill, patience, and service rather than on fighting. Readers get a wholesome adventure for young scouts, showing how the scout code guides a young adult as well as a boy in camp.
20008-the-young-duke:
The Young Duke was Disraeli's novel of 1831, a tale of fashionable life. Its hero inherits a dukedom, wealth, and every temptation young. The Countess in these pages had accepted a diamond bracelet the year before. Such gifts map the novel's world of favors and debts. The Lord Viscount St. Maurice stands as future chief of the Fitz-Pompey house. Names themselves arrive dressed for the season. Disraeli wrote society from inside its ballrooms.

Disraeli was twenty-six, dandified, and in debt when he wrote it. The silver-fork novel, fiction of high life, was his first stage. Dukes, races, and romances fill The Young Duke knowingly. Later statesmanship makes the frivolity fascinating. Hints of ambition already glitter under the pleasure. It is a prime minister's juvenilia, shameless and bright.
20809-archie-s-mistake:
Mill hands at Longcross guard their place with pride in Archie's Mistake. New men they dislike get no peace until they quit the Fairfax mills. To belong there counts as a prize the old hands grant with care.

G. A. Henty wrote tales of mill and factory life under the name here tied to Archie. A wrong step by a newcomer sparks the strife of the tale. Work, pride, and fairness clash on the shop floor. The story shows a less known side of its era's fiction, where mills, not battlefields, test a young man's grit and growth.
21487-the-boy-who-sailed-with-blake:
Robert Blake, the great admiral of the Commonwealth, anchors W. H. G. Kingston's The Boy Who Sailed with Blake. Blake lived from 1599 to 1657 and came late to the sea. He defended Bristol, Lyme Regis, and Taunton in the Civil War before taking command afloat.

Kingston frames the history as a page from the fight for civil and religious liberty. A boy's view carries readers through Blake's wars with Prince Rupert and the Dutch. Blake broke Dutch power at Portland and swept the Barbary coast. The tale avoids cheap heroics, aiming instead at sober pride in hard duty.
21703-silver-lake:
Deep in the North American backwoods, hunter Robin Gore builds a new home for his family in this adventure novel by R. M. Ballantyne. Robin grows tired of settlement life as crowds close in around his hamlet. He moves his wife, his son Roy, and his daughter Nelly hundreds of miles into the wild woods, past the last farms.

His nephew Walter and an Irishman named Larry O'Dowd go along to build the new settlement. The family raises three wooden huts and rings them with a stockade for safety. Ballantyne knew the northern woods from his own years in Canada, and the hunting, weather, and daily work here feel close and real.
23256-the-king-of-beaver-and-beaver-ligh:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The King of Beaver and Beaver Lights comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories. Its subject is James Strang, who styled himself King and Prophet of a peculiar sect on Beaver Island. In the state legislature, Strang had learned how to handle men in the mass.

Nature had also doubly fitted him to entrance women, the tale notes. The spiritual side of Strang appealed most to the one listener best able to appreciate him. Catherwood treats a real island kingdom with a storyteller's eye. Readers get frontier faith, ambition, and charm mixed in one unsettling figure.
23732-a-girl-of-the-klondike:
Victoria Cross published A Girl of the Klondike in America through the Macaulay Company, after its first appearance abroad. Its epigraph asks, in Latin, what the cursed hunger for gold does not drive mortal hearts to do. The answer plays out in Alaska, where night falls black over snow wastes, ice-fields, and the fettered Yukon.

Katrine, the girl of the title, moves through a night in town, the West Gulch, and neighbors whose lives gold has bent. Chapters titled God's Gift, Gold-Plated, and Mammon's Pay trace how greed, love, and cruelty contend in the gold country. Cross writes in a lush, intense style, and the Klondike she shows is as much a moral landscape as a frozen one.
23738-the-thing-from-the-lake:
Eleanor M. Ingram published The Thing from the Lake in 1921, a supernatural novel with a careful distinction at its start. Its narrator, Mr. Locke, insists this is not the story of a haunted house. It is the story of a beleaguered house, besieged as Prague was in legend by a midnight army of spectres.

Locke first sees the place through a real-estate agent's eyes: a dilapidated Connecticut farm with woodland, farm land, a lake, and a double row of maples. Spring rain whispers from a gray sky as he surveys it. What he takes for a bargain summer home soon shows itself as something else, and the lake at its edge holds the key to the siege.
23927-a-tame-surrender-a-story-of-the-ch:
Captain Charles King published A Tame Surrender, A Story of the Chicago Strike, in Philadelphia in 1896. Its heroine, Miss Allison, first met her young man the previous summer on the Rhine. Now, her friends say, they count as good as engaged, since he follows her everywhere.

Miss Allison is undersized one way and oversized another, her brother jokes: not more than five feet high, nor less than five feet broad, measured across her fashionable wings. Her wings are fashion, not angelhood, billowing from her shoulders like balloons. Against the Chicago strike, King sets a romance of soldiers, despatches, and a surrender that is tame only in name.
24587-the-lowest-rung-together-with-the-:
Mary Cholmondeley, author of Red Pottage, published this story collection at London in 1908, dedicated to Howard Sturgis. Its four stories are The Lowest Rung, The Hand on the Latch, St. Luke's Summer, and The Understudy. The title story opens after a night of hurricane, as sun breaks through racing clouds over water meadows.

Cholmondeley writes of English country life, with wit, feeling, and a sharp eye for character. Her people climb and slip down fortune's ladder, rung by rung, as Kipling's epigraph warns. Readers who enjoy Edwardian tales of manners and morals will find this collection quietly powerful.
25002-roy-blakeley-s-bee-line-hike:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh's 1922 Boy Scout story, illustrated by R. Emmett Owen and published with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America, sends Roy Blakeley and his patrol on a bee-line hike. The chapters chart the trip's mishaps and jokes: losing a member, missionary work, a solemn pledge, a stumbling block, famine, reel adventure, diplomacy, eats, bandits and things, and a haunted wheel. A scout is observant, suspense builds, and a hero emerges before the final dash.

Midway through the hike, talk turns to a boat found in the marshes near Bridgeboro. A fellow may be hiding around Northvale, three or four miles up the river, where a boat club stands. The men who came looking row back against the tide, and Roy muses that he would like to be a detective, though not a truant officer. The book is pure patrol high spirits.
25562-william-adolphus-turnpike:
William Banks writes this 1913 novel about William Adolphus Turnpike, a city boy teased for never having been to a political meeting. His father belongs to the executive of the Ward Eighteen Conservative Club, so politics runs in the family talk.

Early chapters show William at work for Mr. Whimple, who soon finds the boy no model of industry, and follow his quick talk and quicker thinking through town life. A front picture shows kindly hands binding up his wounds, hinting at scrapes ahead. Banks keeps the voice colloquial, comic, and warm.
25612-the-art-or-crafte-of-rhetoryke:
The Art or Crafte of Rhetoryke, first published about 1530 with a second edition in 1532, stands as the first book on rhetoric in English. This text follows the 1532 edition from microfiche scans held by the Bibliotheque nationale de France.

Old spelling, capitalisation, and punctuation are kept, including a spaced slash for the comma and u for v, i for j, as in Tudor print. Apparent printer errors are kept too and listed at the end. The book teaches speakers how to frame, order, and adorn speech, founding English rhetoric in plain, practical rules.
262-the-collected-poems-of-rupert-brooke:
Rupert Brooke died in the Aegean in April 1915, aged twenty-seven, and became a symbol of a lost generation. The Collected Poems, in the 1915 edition, gathers his lyrics with an introduction by George Edward Woodberry and a biographical note. Brooke's life runs from Rugby to Cambridge to war.

His poems move from love and youth to the soldier's sonnets that made him famous. An appendix adds poems written about or to Brooke by others. The volume preserves the vivid, charming voice his friends recalled. It remains a poignant record of promise cut short.
27187-a-warwickshire-lad-the-story-of-th:
George Madden Martin's A Warwickshire Lad, published by Appleton in 1916, imagines the boyhood of William Shakespeare. The illustrations show Will clambering on a settle to think, his father tweaking his ear, and Gammer telling tales, with the birthplace as frontispiece.

Young Will sees the players, declares he shall be a player too, and walks to his grandfather's at Snitterfield, meeting Bardolph the tapster and wandering the river banks. Martin builds a gentle, homely Stratford boyhood for the playwright, from cattle-buying to first dreams of the stage. The book was copyrighted in 1903 by P. F. Collier and Son before the 1916 Appleton edition.
28287-the-lady-of-the-lake:
Sir Walter Scott's The Lady of the Lake, in the Lake English Classics revised edition edited by William Vaughn Moody, is a school text of Scott's famous poem. Scott, born in Edinburgh on August 15, 1771, of a Border clan of hard riders. He sets the poem in the Trossachs, where Ellen, Roderick Dhu, and James Fitz-James meet by lake and glen. Scott, Foresman and Company published the edition in 1919.

Moody's helps to study, notes, themes, and class readings guide pupils through Scott's place in the Romantic movement. The poem's historical setting and general criticism open the volume. The book suits students meeting Scott's Highland romance for the first time.
28517-hepsey-burke:
Frank N. Westcott's Hepsey Burke, published by the H. K. Fly Company of New York in 1915 with illustrations by Frederick R. Gruger, opens with a young man arriving by train. The station-master offers a ride on the ice wagon, since the bus will not come until the next train. The visitor stands on a platform beside a little curb-roofed building shaped like Noah's Ark.

Later chapters follow gossip, the senior warden, milking, a miniature, a missionary tea, and Hepsey going fishing. An icebox for Cherubim, the rectory, a bride's arrival, a circus, and Hepsey's diplomacy fill the parish comedy. Readers get a warm, talkative novel of village church life.
28876-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
David Widger edited this linked index to Gaston Maspero's History of Egypt, Chaldaea, Syria, Babylonia, and Assyria, in thirteen volumes. Volume one opens with the Nile and Egypt, the gods of Egypt, and the legendary history of Egypt, with one hundred seventy pictures. Volume two treats the political constitution of Egypt and the Memphite and Theban empires.

Later volumes move through ancient Chaldaea, its temples and civilization, the first Chaldaean empire, and Syria at the beginning of the second millennium. The index lists every chapter and special plate, from mummy wrappings to the pyramid of Khephren. Readers get a guide to Maspero's great history, a classic of Egyptology that still rewards browsing.
29304-in-the-days-of-drake:
J. S. Fletcher published this historical novel in Chicago and New York in 1897. Fletcher's introduction calls the Elizabethan age the most heroic period in English history, when good Queen Bess ruled English hearts and Englishmen set out on great ventures by land and sea. Drake's day, he writes, was an age of personal valor and marvelous courage.

The novel's chapters open with the narrator's home, friends, and surroundings, then bring in Pharaoh Nanjulian, foul play, and schemes and stratagems. Fletcher, author of When Charles I Was King, writes adventure in the heroic mode. Readers get a late Victorian boys' romance of Elizabethan England, full of daring deeds and sea-going enterprise.
29322-when-the-sleepers-woke:
Arthur Leo Zagat published this story in Astounding Stories in November 1932. Only two small enemy groups live on amid the vast desolation of the Final War. Allan Dane, a pilot in a one-man helicopter, hears the crackling command in his helmet: prepare for battle, enemy approaching from the southeast, squadron commanders execute plan two.

Dane's squadron waits in reserve while the American air fleet moves over New York and its bay. Suddenly movement ceases and the formation freezes, ten flying forts, each crowning a far-spread cone. Zagat builds a future war from fleets, forts, and waiting pilots. Readers get a pulp tale of the last war's survivors, where two remnant peoples fight on over a ruined world.
29617-the-vagrant-duke:
George Gibbs's Vagrant Duke, printed by D. Appleton and Company of New York, opens with a prologue, then introduces Peter Nichols, New York, and the overall girl. Later chapters take up the job, new elements, the house of terror, music, the placard, and a character called Hawk. Ancient history, confession, the chase, and two letters close the tale. A picture shows Peter striking a man full on the head.

Gibbs, author of The Splendid Outcast and The Yellow Dove, writes a popular romance of rank, disguise, and American life. The vagrant duke of the title wanders between worlds. Readers of early twentieth-century romantic fiction will find a lively, well-plotted tale of a duke adrift.
29859-dave-porter-at-bear-camp-or-the-wi:
Edward Stratemeyer published Dave Porter at Bear Camp in Boston in 1915, with pictures by Walter S. Rogers. The boys start on shipboard, with something about the past and a rescue at sea, before they return to Crumville and Dave's home. News of importance and Link Merwell again set the plot moving. Then the party sets off for Bear Camp, on the road and caught in a storm.

A stroke of lightning, a quarrel, visitors, and a strange communication follow at camp. A swimming race, a cry from the cliff, and the capture of Link Merwell raise the stakes. An escape, a wildcat shot, and a man at the cabin deepen the mystery of Mirror Lake. The wild man of the title waits at the heart of a brisk boys' camp tale.
30063-double-take:
Richard Wilson wrote Double Take, with pictures by Paul Orban. Its headnote promises that the barn turned out to be a spaceship in disguise, and that was only the beginning. Young Paul Asher found himself going around in circles, very peculiar circles indeed. Paul Asher, twenty-seven, a men's furnishings buyer, leans back as a cloth band is fastened across his chest, adjusts his heavy spectacles, breathes deeply, and is off.

He shoots out of a tunnel into dazzling sunlight, driving a high-powered vehicle up a long rising curve toward a mountaintop city. He thinks he is alone in the car. He is not. A pretty girl with dark hair and a wide red mouth in a half smile tells him to keep going, sweetheart, as fast as he can. She pats the oversized pocketbook in her lap.
3011-the-lady-of-the-lake:
Sir Walter Scott wrote The Lady of the Lake as a narrative poem of the Scottish Highlands, set around Loch Katrine. This edition, edited with notes by William Rolfe of Cambridge, Massachusetts, was prepared for school and household use from an illustrated edition. Rolfe notes the trouble of fixing Scott's text, since even the so-called author's edition proved unreliable at the start.

The poem follows Ellen Douglas, her father, and the king in disguise through hunts, battles, and clan loyalty. A hound named Lufra, fondly bred to share the Douglas board and watch his bed, suffers a huntsman's blow after a hunt is broken short. The Lady of the Lake remains Scott's most musical romance, famous for its Highland scenery and its galloping verse.
30247-mabel-s-mistake:
Mrs. Ann S. Stephens offers Mabel's Mistake in a Peterson volume from Philadelphia, entered in 1868, priced at a dollar seventy-five in cloth and a dollar fifty in paper cover. An epigraph verse imagines something purer far and freer from stain, where friendship, love, and passion still remain human, and bids the reader ask angels for its name. Stephens lists the novel among a shelf of popular works, from The Curse of Gold and Wives and Widows to The Rejected Wife and The Heiress.

Each work stands complete in one duodecimo volume, sold by all booksellers and sent postage prepaid on receipt of price. Mabel's Mistake belongs to Stephens's sensation and domestic mode, where a single error, as the title warns, can unsettle a life. Readers of her earlier successes will find the same strong feeling, clear incident, and steady moral pressure at work.
3286-selections-from-the-speeches-and-wr:
This volume selects the speeches and writings of Edmund Burke, the great eighteenth-century parliamentarian. An introductory essay opens with Quintilian's rule. He who would be an orator must be a good man. His authority makes dissent feel shameful, and he brings a witness's faith rather than an advocate's zeal. Burke is offered as that kind of speaker.

The selections range across his career: America, France, India, and the nature of government itself. A sharp line in the essay calls democracy the most monstrous of all governments, because it cannot at once act and control. Readers get Burke's rhetoric whole: long periods, moral passion, and a conservatism rooted in history rather than in mere resistance to change.
32880-death-makes-a-mistake:
P. F. Costello gives Death himself a bookkeeping error, in a story from Amazing Stories of January 1943. Reggie Van Fiddler saunters into the Midland Club in an exceptionally amiable mood, bound for long cool drinks at the bar. He slept until twelve thirty, which explains why the glorious morning is already gone.

At the bar a small, dark, narrow-eyed man watches him with a steady fixed stare. Warmed by alcohol and a lurid imagination, Reggie decides after four drinks that the stranger must be an Axis agent. The stranger is Mr. Demise, and Reggie's name stands in his book. Demise vanishes into thin air before Reggie's eyes, then reappears to prove it. Reggie sets out to correct the mistake, and by the end a grateful Demise promises he will not slip up on this one.
34404-the-beautiful-miss-brooke:
The Beautiful Miss Brooke, by Louis Zangwill, was published by Appleton at New York in 1897. The front pages carry press praise of his earlier work, with London papers calling him one of the ablest novelists of the day. The tale opens at a ball, where Paul Middleton has been bored by a partner and counts the dances owed to Celia.

Five dances on Celia's programme and supper with her hold him at the house. He toys with slipping away to a chess club and an important match he had given up for the evening. His hostess is his mother's oldest friend, which binds him to stay.
34691-hoofbeats-on-the-turnpike:
Hoofbeats on the Turnpike is a girl sleuth tale by Mildred Wirt, out in nineteen forty-four. It is one of a set of such tales past a girl news hand. A front list shows the whole row of those tales, from a witch doll tale to a cry at the dark hour. Past twenty heads fill this book, from an old man of the hills to a big tale.

The tale opens as a girl in creased cloth slacks skids to a halt on the sleek floor of a news house desk room. Past a grin she thrusts a slip past the bars of the coin mans cage. She greets him with a bright call and asks him to cash a small check for her. The bald, tired man peers at the crisp slip and shakes his head with rue, for his rules bar it.
35486-the-great-gold-rush-a-tale-of-the-:
Jarvis dedicated this tale of the Klondike to Colonel Samuel Benfield Steele, once commander of the North-West Mounted Police in the Yukon. Macmillan published it at Toronto in 1913, and Jarvis had written Letters of a Remittance Man before it. His first chapter sorts the stampeders into tenderfeet and old-timers. The novice catches the fever and dreams dreams. The old-timer goes because his last diggings proved no good.

John Berwick, an experienced man, sails from Vancouver on the steamer Aleutian in March 1898. Ahead lie the trail, the summit in storm, and Dawson at the flood of the rush. The contents name Soapy's little game, graft, a lottery, and revolution plotted against the Mounted Police. Jarvis ends, as the contents promise, with reunion and a happy ending, but only after no surrender in the barracks.
36724-dutch-the-diver-or-a-man-s-mistake:
George Manville Fenn wrote Dutch the Diver, or A Man's Mistake, in a London edition dated eighteen eighty-three. The tale opens at a diver's office, where a young draughtsman named Pug spars with Rasp, the old stoker. Rasp heaps coals on the fire while Pug begs him to stop, and the heat drives their talk. Rasp is sixty and calls himself far from old.

Rasp has worn diving suits for forty years and had his head blown full of wind on job after job. He has risked his life below again and again, and he says the work would make any man cross. Pug laughs that his own many descents have left him mild. Their banter sets up a tale of diving work, risk, and a man's mistake.
37337-my-lord-duke:
Hornung writes a society tale in My Lord Duke, printed in New York in 1897. Scribner made the novel, with copyright the same year. Twenty two chapters carry the story of a young man and a title.

The head of the family leads, then Happy Jack and a chance lost. Not in the programme and with the elect fill the early run. A new leaf and the duke's progress turn the tale. The old Adam, an anonymous letter, and dead nuts raise the stakes. The night of the twentieth and the wrong man bring a crisis. An interregnum follows, then Jack and his master, and the end of the interregnum. Love the gift, heckling a minister, and the cat and the mouse fill the late run. Chapter one opens on a golf party spoiled: the Home Secretary leant his clubs against a chair, with the longest face of all.
37852-chimneysmoke:
Chimneysmoke, a book of poems by Christopher Morley, was published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1927, with drawings by Thomas Fogarty. Many of the verses were reprinted from three earlier Morley books. Those books are Songs for a Little House from 1917, The Rocking Horse from 1919, and Hide and Seek from 1920. One piece goes back to an early Oxford venture of 1912.

The poems turn on hearth, home, and small joys. A verse at the front builds the fireside scene: logs sawn, the largest chair drawn to the chimney, the match lit. Morley thanks Fogarty, saying the book rests its claim to be new on the drawings. A line from Kipling on fires stands as motto.
3834-hassan-the-story-of-hassan-of-bagda:
James Elroy Flecker wrote this verse play about Hassan of Baghdad and his golden journey to Samarkand. The action moves through streets, fountains, and palace rooms, where the Caliph, his vizier Jafar, and the swordsman Masrur wait out a crisis with jokes about fate. Hassan studies the ugliness of a carpet pattern while Jafar meditates on the mutability of human affairs and Masrur sharpens his sword on his thigh.

The play blends the Arabian Nights with a modern poet's irony, as a paper thrust into a wall crack and a balcony without a balcony decide a man's fate. Flecker keeps the verse musical and the comedy dry. Readers who like poetic drama will find Hassan a strange and charming work, half fairy tale and half meditation on desire.
39856-expositor-s-bible-the-gospel-of-st:
Henry Burton's volume on the Gospel of Luke belongs to the Expositor's Bible series, edited by Robertson Nicoll and published by Hodder and Stoughton at London. Twenty-six chapters walk through the Gospel in order.

Burton opens by comparing the four Gospels to the four walls and twelve gates of the Seer's city, guarding one City of God. Chapters treat the mute priest, the Gospel psalms, the virgin mother, and the shepherds' adoration. Later chapters cover the Good Samaritan, the two sisters, lost and found, the watch in Gethsemane, and the first Lord's day. Each chapter expounds its passage for preachers and students.
39857-marmaduke:
Flora Annie Steel's Marmaduke was published in New York in 1917 by the Stokes company, printed in Great Britain. Steel had written On the Face of the Waters and King-Errant before it. The tale opens in broad Aberdeenshire speech, with a young officer home again and overjoyed at the sight of old friends.

He hails Davie Sim, then turns to Marrion, tall and still by the window, and marvels at how the child has grown. Many a man, she answers coolly, has told her that and craved kisses since she and Mr Duke were children together. The chill in that greeting sets the terms: old fondness on his side, a guarded pride on hers.
40585-comrades-on-river-and-lake:
Comrades on River and Lake is a boys' adventure by Ralph Victor. Platt and Peck published it in New York in 1910. Schneider drew the illustrations. The book belongs to a long Comrades series. Its heroes are cadets of Winton Hall. Earlier volumes took them to camp, ranch, and school.

Twenty-five chapters pace the summer trip. The comrades leave Winton as commencement nears. A race and a fight on a catboat open the fun. A baseball game fills two chapters ashore. Lake Champlain hosts a fight on the water. The Richelieu River and Montreal follow. The Thousand Islands come at last. A mystery around a lodge deepens midway. Revenue officers and a capture close the plot. The boys return to Mortonville in the end.
40586-billie-bradley-and-her-classmates-:
Billie Bradley and Her Classmates, by Janet Wheeler, was printed in 1921. Cupples and Leon issued it at New York. Its second title runs: The Secret of the Locked Tower. Wheeler had written other Billie Bradley books in the series. Twenty five chapters make the tale. Chapter one is called Thin Ice. Three pairs of skates click over a frozen lake. Billie Bradley laughs at the glory of it: the lake froze in mid November. Violet Farrington warns that the ice is solid only in spots. Laura Jordon asks, anxious, whether thin ice lies ahead.

The girls attend Three Towers Hall, a boarding school on Lake Molata. Later heads promise a cave, an accusation, and a blood-stained handkerchief. The tower room and a stolen secret drive the close.
40921-grim-the-story-of-a-pike:
Svend Fleuron wrote a Danish tale of a pike, put into English by Muir and Alexander and printed at New York in 1921 with drawings by Dorothy Lathrop. A stark motto heads the book. To eat others and to shun being eaten, it says, is the end and aim of life.

Fifteen chapters follow the fish from birth. Life, the shelter of the creek, and first roving open the tale. Robbers, a pearly fish, and a man roach follow. The angler's end, a wedding feast, and terror in the marsh mark the middle. A fight with an otter and an angler from town end the heads. The baby pike lies in warm mud, no longer than a finger.
41237-in-search-of-a-siberian-klondike:
In Search of a Siberian Klondike is a gold-hunting tale told by Washington Vanderlip. Homer Hulbert set forth the story of the chief actor in print. The Century Company brought the book out in October 1903. Many photographs back the tale of the far north-east of Asia. Vanderlip planned to prospect through Kamchatka north to Bering Strait.

Rumour of gold in north-eastern Asia launched the whole hard venture. Saghalien and its convict station at Korsakovsk fill the second chapter. Most prisoners there were murderers, yet freedom was loosely allowed them. The steamer wrecked and the outfit was lost in that early leg. Petropaulovsk and southern Kamchatka gave copper, but no gold at all. Mosquitoes drove the party off the land in that summer season. Salmon fishing in the far north and Ghijiga town fill later parts.
43509-the-motor-boys-across-the-plains-o:
Motor Boys Across the Plains, or the Hermit of Lost Lake, is a boys' novel. Clarence Young wrote it for the Motor Boys series of tales. Cupples and Leon of New York issued the volume in that series. A front plate shows a bear trying to climb on the engine hood. Other series titles cover Mexico, an overland trip, and chums in trouble.

Young also wrote the Jack Ranger school tales for the same market. Each Motor Boys volume sold at sixty cents, postpaid, in cloth. Motoring boys cross the plains and meet a hermit at Lost Lake. Peril, machines, and open country mix in the series formula at work. Boys of that day read of cars as their fathers read of horses.
44450-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Volume nine of The World's Great Sermons runs from Cuyler to Van Dyke, in a set of ten volumes. Grenville Kleiser made the set, with help from famed preachers of the day. Funk and Wagnalls put it out at New York and London, with rights held in 1908. Each preacher gets a sermon and a life note. Cuyler leads with The Value of Life, and Broadus gives Let Us Have Peace with God. Wilberforce speaks on the mother church, and Spalding on learning and the future of faith.

More sermons treat Christ as the question of the centuries, faith that builds, and death as a path to glory. Stalker takes up temptation, Burrell tells how to become a Christian, and Watson preaches optimism. Nicoll gives Gethsemane as the rose garden of God. The book gives pulpit voice at its height.
45888-scott-s-lady-of-the-lake:
Helen E Bacon edited Scott's Lady of the Lake for schools. The American Book Company issued it in its Eclectic English Classics line. Copyright dates run 1893 and 1910. A map shows the poem's places up front. An intro tells Scott's own life first. Scott was ninth of twelve children, it says.

Edinburgh saw his birth in August 1771. A lame, frail child, he went to Sandyknowe young. His grandfather's shepherd laid him by the crags there. Open air built his strength on those hills. A slight limp stayed with him for life. Kelso and Edinburgh schooled the sturdy boy. Tasso and Percy's Reliques woke his love of wild beauty. A school edition with life and notes put Scotland's great verse tale into class rooms across America.
46264-songs-from-the-smoke:
Madeleine Sweeny Miller wrote Songs from the Smoke, a book of poems published by the Methodist Book Concern in 1914. Miller, a Vassar graduate, lived with the smoke of Pittsburgh in view. Her foreword tells of a noted Pittsburgh composer who tried for years to catch the spirit of the Steel City in music and failed.

The poems fall into three parts. Songs for the Brothers Who Toil treats mill hands, immigrants, delivery boys, and rain at the mill. Songs for the Evening Hour turns to faith, memory, and the burning of Chambersburg. Songs for the Seasons closes the book with pieces on Easter, Christmas, spring, and winter apples. Miller writes of hard city labor with sympathy and hope, asking readers to see beauty and worth in working lives.
4730-the-songs-of-a-sentimental-bloke:
C. J. Dennis wrote The Songs of a Sentimental Bloke in Australian verse, with a French epigraph on life as a little love, a little hate, and then good day. A foreword writer says Dennis asked him to preface the book, though a man can best preface his own book, whether he knows it good or bad. While running in the Bulletin, the Bloke brightened many dark days for that writer.

The Bloke, he says, is more perfect than any larrikin or Bottle-O character he ever sketched, not excepting his own Benno. Take the first poem, where the Bloke gets the hump, a longing for something better, felt by men in many lands and languages. Readers get a humorous, tender verse tale of an Australian larrikin in love, in slangy, musical lines, with a glossary of local terms to help outsiders follow the fun.
5091-the-tempting-of-tavernake:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Tempting of Tavernake opens in despair and interest on a London boarding-house roof near Russell Square. The house is a grim shelter for Transatlantic curiosity and British penury. A girl, representing the former, leans against frail palisading with gloomy expression, contemplating an uninspiring panorama.

A young man, unmistakably and uncompromisingly English, stands with his back to a chimney a few feet away. He watches her in a silence unbroken since she stole from the shabby drawing room below. Oppenheim builds a romance of temptation from that rooftop meeting. Readers get an Edwardian tale of money, love, and moral choice, beginning above the city's roofs.
51414-so-they-baked-a-cake:
So They Baked a Cake is a science fiction story by Winston Marks, taken from Dynamic Science Fiction for January 1954. The narrator is a human-interest columnist who has grown tired of people. He specializes in glamorizing the commonplace and the sordid, and he hates the work. The first starship seems to offer him the ideal escape from it all.

He and his fellow pioneers are the first to try the Larson Drive in deep space. Their destination lies twenty-six trillion miles away, down near the celestial south pole. It is not much more than a parsec, but a parsec nonetheless, and for the first time human travel would be measured in parsecs. The narrator's private qualification for the job, he says, was simply being fed up with humanity. He lists his grievances: bureaucracy, rationing, synthetic food, and standing in line.
53375-occoneechee-the-maid-of-the-mystic:
Occoneechee, the Maid of the Mystic Lake is a long poem on the Cherokee by Robert Frank Jarrett. The Shakespeare Press published the work at New York in 1916. Jarrett had issued Back Home and Other Poems five years before. A short life of the author opens the volume.

Jarrett writes in his preface that a nation's memory lives in its songs. He hopes to keep the once powerful Cherokee in mind for ages to come. The poem falls into parts on the nation, on Occoneechee herself, and on Cherokee myths. A word list of Cherokee terms closes the book. Jarrett was born at Asheville in North Carolina in 1864. He learned his craft, he says, in field and forest by rippling streams. The poem is a mountain man's tribute to his native hills and their first people.
54215-the-life-of-sophia-jex-blake:
Margaret Todd, a doctor writing also as Graham Travers, wrote The Life of Sophia Jex-Blake for Macmillan at London in 1918. The dedication thanks all who lent a helping hand to a brave and unselfish fighter. Part one follows childhood and a stormy school life: home letters, holidays, a confession, and a departure from school. Life at home, dreams of authorship, and friendship with Octavia Hill lead to Queen's College, where Jex-Blake became a mathematics tutor.

The fight over payment for her work, a certificate won with great credit, and a first Edinburgh visit fill the middle chapters. The life is that of the leader of the Edinburgh women who fought to study medicine and qualify as doctors. Todd uses letters and diaries throughout, and a portrait shows Jex-Blake at twenty-five. The contents promise the German and Edinburgh medical campaigns in the parts beyond.
56899-the-vicar-of-morwenstow-being-a-li:
A life of Robert Stephen Hawker by S Baring-Gould. Methuen published this new and revised edition at London in 1899. Hawker was vicar of Morwenstow, on the Cornish coast. He was also a poet of strange, fervent gifts. A French epigraph calls him admirable and ill-balanced. It says he lived inside a romance of his own making.

Baring-Gould knew the Cornish world he describes. Hawker built his parish a famous carved church and vicarage. He salvaged drowned sailors and gave them Christian burial. Eccentric dress and opium marked his later years. Ballads like the Song of the Western Men made him famous. This biography, by a fellow novelist and antiquarian, remains the standard life. Asterisks mark names changed to protect the living.
574-poems-of-william-blake:
William Blake's Songs of Innocence and of Experience anchor this poetry volume, with The Book of Thel beside them. The Shepherd, The Echoing Green, and the piper's opening song set the innocent world: lambs, children, and green fields under a kind shepherd. Experience answers with darker songs of city, church, and woe.

Blake writes in short, musical lines, pairing innocence and experience as two contrary states of the soul. His plain diction hides deep vision. The book serves as a fine entry to Blake, where a child's song can carry a prophet's charge.
57508-the-camp-fire-girls-at-half-moon-l:
Camp Fire Girls at Half Moon Lake is a girls novel by Margaret Vandercook. The John Winston Company of Philadelphia issued it in nineteen twenty one. Vandercook also wrote the Ranch Girls and Red Cross Girls series books. This title stands thirteenth in the Camp Fire Girls list order.

Chapters open with Indian summer, the lake, and old friends reunited there. A hermit, a talk and a loss, and a man for all that follow. The poet corner, holiday guests, and Juliet Temple fill the middle chapters. Anxious waiting and Christmas Eve build toward romance and an encounter. Closed in, then spring, ends the camp tale in eighteen chapters.
58646-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Edmund Burke, compiled by David Widger, lists the Burke texts in the Gutenberg library and reproduces their tables of contents. Thoughts on the Present Discontents heads the list, followed by speeches and writings and the twelve volumes of the Works.

Samples show the index at work. A study edition of the speech on conciliation with America gives its apparatus. A preface, an introduction, Burke as a statesman, and groups of writers before, with, and after Burke. Topics for special reports, and a bibliography. Then the speech itself, delivered in the Commons on March 22, 1775. Selections from the speeches and writings are tabled under headwords. The nature and functions of the Commons, Newton and nature, the sublime, obscurity, and the beautiful. Ambition, influence of the crown, voice of the people, and dozens more.
58925-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of John Fiske, the American historian and philosopher. The file is a finding aid rather than a book by Fiske himself. It lists his works as Gutenberg issued them, then prints the table of contents of each volume in turn. Readers can see at a glance what each book holds before opening it.

The list runs from Myths and Myth-Makers through The Discovery of America and The American Revolution. Old Virginia and Her Neighbours, The Beginnings of New England, and The War of Independence all appear. So do essays on religion and thought, such as The Unseen World and Through Nature to God. Fiske wrote widely on America's colonial past and on evolution and belief. Widger's index gathers that whole shelf into one place and serves anyone working through the Gutenberg editions of a once famous author.
59118-ye-sundial-booke:
T Geoffrey W Henslow compiles Ye Sundial Booke at London in 1914, dedicating it in verse to Wiltshire men. Contents open with the history of the sundial and photographs of a Saxon sundial built into the south porch of a Norman church at Stanton, near Chippenham, which Henslow himself discovered. Famous men and the sundial, with notes on mottoes, and a chapter on setting a dial follow.

Most of the book is verses and sketches: poems on the sundial, the dial's motto, the maid and the sundial, running to page 402 with additional mottoes. A closing list names places where sundials exist, with an index to sketches and verses.
59541-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of William Locke is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. It gathers, in one file, the tables of contents of all of Locke's novels then available from Project Gutenberg. Readers of the free library could see at a glance what each book contains.

Twenty novels are listed. Simon the Jester, The Red Planet, The Fortunate Youth and The Morals of Marcus Ordeyne come first, each with its full chapter list. Viviette, Septimus, Jaffery and the Adventures of Aristide Pujol follow. Far-Away Stories, At the Gate of Samaria, Stella Maris and A Study in Shadows continue the roll. Where Love Is, Derelicts, The White Dove, The Demagogue and Lady Phayre, and Idols complete it, with The Belovéd Vagabond, The Mountebank and The Rough Road added. Locke, a bestselling novelist of sentiment and adventure, is here reduced to a shelf list.
60255-roy-blakeley-s-funny-bone-hike:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Roy Blakeley's Funny-Bone Hike, copyrighted in New York in 1923, with pictures by Barbour. The book came out with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Fitzhugh had written the Tom Slade books and Roy Blakeley. A front picture shows Roy tumbling out with all of them after him. Thirty-six chapters and a chapter the last carry the hike, each headed in the same we-form.

We go, we start back, we go south, we go north: the heads run on in that vein. The troop reaches the fickle guide post, does a good turn, and is marooned on a desert island. They cook the duck, hear a voice, go to the rescue, and lose their bearings. They become bandits, win, start the parade, and end the hike. Roy calls it the craziest story he ever wrote.
60448-william-blake:
Arthur Symons wrote a study of William Blake published at New York in 1907 and dedicated to Auguste Rodin, whose work he calls the marriage of heaven and hell. Part one introduces Blake and his art. Part two gathers records from contemporary sources. Henry Crabb Robinson's diary, letters, and reminiscences lead the records, transcribed from the manuscripts in Dr Williams's Library.

Benjamin Heath Malkin's memoir of his child follows, with Blake material from 1806. Lady Charlotte Bury's diary of 1820 and Blake's horoscope of 1825 appear. Obituary notices from 1827 close the documents. Symons was an early champion of Blake for modern readers.
60946-mindsnake:
Mindsnake, a science fiction tale by Jim Harmon, ran in Worlds of If in November 1960. Hammen walks a crowded ramp on a strange planet with his dog Lad at his heels, while walkers cry witch at him. He wears the word like a badge of honor now, though it tastes of brass. Lad speaks with him in thought and cannot grasp how anyone could hate his master.

Crowds fresh from the transmatter stations mix nudists, cavaliers, and moss-covered folk out for novelty. Hammen walks by choice under his own power, even to the stars. Hale and Lora, a polished blond pair, greet him, and talk turns to trouble held back for a fit time. Telepathy, pets, and spite shape the tale.
61410-an-attempt-to-analyse-the-automato:
An unnamed writer tries to analyze the automaton chess player of Kempelen in this pamphlet, printed at London in 1821. An easy method of imitating the figure's movements is promised in the title. Original drawings illustrate the attempt, drawn on stone by the author himself in the plates.

A copious collection of the knight's moves over the chess board is added to the work. The Turk, a turbaned figure that played chess against all comers, had puzzled Europe for fifty years. Writers guessed at a child, a dwarf or magnets inside, and this analysis picks at the cabinet's secret with diagrams and reason.
61938-the-burston-school-strike:
Casey, a writer for the Labour Leader, wrote this penny booklet on the Burston school strike, in an edition from the National Labour Press dated 1915. It is dedicated to the brave women of Burston, who had struggled since April 1914 against what the writer calls the tyranny of the countryside. The preface calls the booklet a protest against injustice.

Burston is a small, religious, law-abiding village in Norfolk. Its people, Casey says, rose against the rector and the squire after years of putting up with their rule. Parents stood by their teachers for fifteen months, were fined again and again, and their children left the Council School, while the fight was still not over.
62804-let-s-cook-meat-recipes-you-ll-lik:
Let Us Cook Meat is a recipe booklet of meat dishes, given out by a Portland market. Phil Thriftway Market of North Killingsworth in Portland sends holiday greetings in its pages. Beef recipes and menus lead, from corned beef and cabbage to standing ribs of beef. Baked beef and rice, chili patties, pot roast, and pepper steak fill that first part.

Veal follows with croquettes, paprika veal, and stuffed veal birds in sour cream styles. Pork closes the set with barbecued chops, smoked ham glazes, and candied ham loaf. Leftovers get their own slots in each meat part of the handy booklet. Home cooks gained a store promo cookbook of tested family dishes here.
63640-jupiter-s-joke:
A L Haley wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1954. Casey Ritter never turned down a dare, its head note says. He breathes a prayer to the gods of idiots and spacemen and heads toward Jupiter's great red spot. Ritter narrates in the first person, in a hard boiled voice.

Solar System Customs caught Ritter smuggling Kooleen crystals in from Mars. The crystals are deadly, and even experiments with them are illegal. Ritter will not inform on the doctor who hired him. Facing a long sentence, he is instead sent to Jupiter by the customs court. He asks if they mean to choke him in chlorine there.
63749-mimsy-s-joke:
Millard Grimes wrote this space tale for Planet Stories, where it ran in March 1954. Its head note shows Nance smiling on the long trip back from Mars. The trip, he thinks, will be one long chuckle over a great, grim, and strange joke.

Oscar Nance is the world's top digger of old ruins, and that is why the call comes. The United Nations picks a crew for Earth's first voyage to Mars, and wants him on it. The tale opens on a spring day at home, his cocker spaniel Mimsy at his ear. He cuffs her fondly and says good-bye. Mimsy, the note hints, may grasp the joke best of all in the end.
64135-vigilante-days-and-ways-the-pionee:
Vigilante Days and Ways, the pioneers of the Rockies and the makers and making of Montana and Idaho, was written by Nathaniel Langford. McClurg printed it at Chicago in 1912, from a copyright of 1890. Langford also wrote on the wonders of Yellowstone. The book is dedicated to the memory of the unknown pioneers who lost their lives laying the foundations of the empire of the new great West.

Fifty one chapters fill the contents. Henry Plummer opens the roll of road agents, followed by society in Lewiston, the northern mines, and the first vigilance committee. Bannack in 1862, Alder Gulch, and Virginia City anchor the Montana story. Coach robberies, the trial and execution of George Ives, and the execution of Plummer mark the vigilantes' height. Later chapters treat Slade, the stage coach, and a closing retrospection.
6468-on-a-torn-away-world-or-the-captive:
Roy Rockwood, author of the Great Marvel series, opens On a Torn Away World with Jack Darrow flicking lacquer drops from a paintbrush and shouting hurrah: the last stroke, she is finished. His chum Mark Sampson, less confident, quotes that proof of pudding lies in eating, not chewing the pudding bag string. The great body before them is the Snowbird, white all over, an airship with emergency wings, also a plane, built through vacation from college for speed and carrying.

A mid passage finds the party walking with an oil man and his sullen Indians toward shacks on a mountainside. They hear a hail from Professor Henderson, Jack Darrow, and Washington White descending behind them. Rockwood writes a boys' marvel tale, where a home built airship carries its crew to a world torn away by earthquake, with captives, chases, and strange lands.
65539-boy-scouts-in-the-white-mountains-:
Walter Prichard Eaton wrote this Boy Scout story, copyrighted in 1914 and published by the Wilde Company of Boston and Chicago, with illustrations by Frank Merrill. Eaton's earlier Scout books, listed at the front, take his boys to the Berkshires, the Dismal Swamp, Glacier Park, and Crater Lake. This one sends them on a long hike over the Franconia and Presidential ranges.

The chapters follow the route peak by peak, from getting ready and a Fourth of July on Kinsman to Moosilauke and Lost River. The Lafayette ridge follows, with a dinner party at the end of that climb. Later chapters cross the forehead of the Old Man of the Mountain, pass Crawford Notch, and fight a storm on the Crawford bridle path. The boys then climb Tuckerman's Ravine and the Huntington head wall, give first aid in the clouds, and come home through King's Ravine.
66993-historical-record-of-the-seventy-s:
Richard Cannon compiled the Historical Record of the Seventy-Second Regiment, the Duke of Albany’s Own Highlanders. Parker, Furnivall, and Parker issued the book in London in eighteen hundred forty eight. Cannon worked at the Adjutant General’s Office at Horse Guards. The series gave each British regiment its own printed past.

The Seventy-Second was raised in seventeen hundred seventy eight. The Earl of Seaforth took command and led it to Elgin. Jersey and Guernsey guards came first in its service. In seventeen hundred eighty one it sailed for the East Indies. Seaforth died on the long sea road to Madras. Cudalore’s storm and peace with Tippoo fill the India years. The word Hindoostan on its colour marks that long tour. Cape of Good Hope, won in eighteen hundred six, marks the next.
67639-william-blake:
Chesterton's William Blake, in the Popular Library of Art from Duckworth of London and Dutton of New York, studies the poet and artist with thirty-three illustrations. The plates follow Blake's work from the Songs of Innocence of 1789 to the whirlwind designs of his last years.

Chesterton opens by saying Blake himself would have understood that any biography should really begin with the creation of the world. The illustrations show The Lamb, The Little Black Boy, The Tyger, and Holy Thursday, then the prophetic books: frontispieces and preludes from America and Urizen. Later plates show the Waters of Life, the Crucifixion, and the Judgment Day. The book gives general readers a life of Blake in short compass, with his strange pictures doing half the talking.
67864-the-story-of-sir-francis-drake:
Elton wrote this life of Drake for the Children's Heroes series, with pictures by Robinson. A frontispiece shows Queen Elizabeth knighting Drake aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford. Philip of Spain opens the contents, and the troublesome voyage follows at page six.

Nombre de Dios, Fort Diego and the golden mule trains fill the treasure chapters in the list. Home again, round the world and Sir Francis come in order after them. Cadiz, the great Armada, an expedition to Lisbon and the last voyage close a sailor's life told for children, from Devon cabin boy to England's sea king.
68410-deny-the-slake:
Deny the Slake is a short tale of space flight by Richard Wilson. It first ran in a science fiction magazine in April of nineteen fifty seven. Art for the tale was drawn by an artist named Gaughan. The plot turns on scraps of verse left by a lost world of men.

A ship crew tries to read rhymes turned from a dead tongue into English. Their word expert warns that the verse will seem dark at first glance. Each short rhyme drips with gloom and a sense of doom for its lost folk. The skipper scoffs at the stuff as mere doggerel and quits for his cabin. The crew must prove that the rhymes hold the cause of a world death.
68601-scarred-eagle-or-moorooine-the-spo:
Scarred Eagle, or Moorooine the Sporting Fawn, is a dime novel of the lakes frontier by Andrew Dearborn. Beadle and Adams published it in New York, entering it for copyright in 1870.

The first chapter, White against Red, opens in mid-chase on Lake Erie. Two rifle shots ring out as five Indigenous warriors in a canoe pursue a second canoe holding a white man and his Indigenous companion. The white man is Scarred Eagle, a border fighter past forty whose body carries the marks of many wounds. One whole side of his face is a single scar, the sign that gave him his name among the peoples who fear and respect him. Chapter heads promise a gorge decoy, beauty in bonds, a bloody trophy, and a forlorn hope.
69970-the-english-husbandman-the-second-:
The Second Booke of the English Husbandman is an old work on farm and garden craft. Its title page sets out its scope in full. It deals with the ordering of the kitchen garden and the planting of strange flowers. It deals as well with the breeding of all kinds of cattle. The cures and the feeding of cattle are treated in its pages.

The ordering of pastures and of meadow ground forms part of the book. So does the use of high wood and of underwood. A treatise called Goodmens Recreation is added at the end. That piece is a talk on the broad art of fishing, as the title page states. A note by the transcriber warns that spellings shift in the text, with old forms of letters kept as they stand in the first print.
70688-rajah-brooke:
Spenser St John wrote a life of James Brooke for the Builders of Greater Britain set, issued in London in 1899. The set was edited by Wilson, a lawyer at the Colonial Office, and this book stands as its seventh life. Brooke ruled Sarawak as an English rajah in the far east.

Brooke was the second son of Thomas Brooke of the Bengal Civil Service and Anna Maria Stuart. He served in Burma, was hurt, and left the army, then cruised in his yacht Royalist to Borneo. Contents trace his trips to Sarawak, a civil war he helped end, his grant of rule, and his fights with pirates of the Seribas.
70780-big-lake:
Lynn Riggs stages sorrow in Big Lake, a tragedy in two parts, printed in New York in 1927. Samuel French made the book, with copyright the same year. The play comes as produced by the American Laboratory Theater of New York City. A photograph shows Helen Coburn as Betty.

The programme of the first production, April 8, 1927, is kept in front. George Auerbach staged the play. Helen Coburn played Betty, Frank Burk played Lloyd, and Stella Adler played Elly. Riggs's other plays are listed with it: Knives from Syria, a comedy in one act, and two pieces not yet published. Acting rights, professional and amateur, are reserved in full, a notice warns. Companies must apply to Samuel French for leave to perform or read it in public.
70893-the-abandoned-farm-and-connie-s-mi:
Mrs Mary J Holmes wrote The Abandoned Farm and Connie Mistake, two tales in one volume from G W Dillingham Company in New York. Copyright rests in nineteen oh one and nineteen oh two, and the issue here is nineteen oh five. Holmes had earlier written Tempest and Sunshine and Lena Rivers. Part one, The Abandoned Farm, runs fourteen chapters. Chapter one is Alex Marsh. Breakfast was late at the Marsh house as it opens.

Alex Marsh, his sister Amy, and a cousin fill the opening house. Alex Letters, Alex and the Pledgers, and Sherry follow. The Interview, Maplehurst, and The Arrival move the tale to a country estate. The Cedar Chest, The Fancy Dance, and The Somnambulist deepen the mystery. Finding the Wrong and Righting the Wrong close part one. Part two tells Connie tale across eighteen chapters. Novel readers get two Holmes romances in one binding.
72179-a-prison-make:
William Stuart wrote this stark tale for Amazing Stories' July 1962 issue, with art by Finlay. Its note claims a Kafka-like cast: the hero stands for Everyman who picks the known horror over the unknown. That likeness, it says, is no accident.

The man on the bunk wakes, but not up. He does not move, save for a half twitch, half shrug. He does not open his eyes. In the grey fog past sleep two things stand sure. There is no hurry at all to open his eyes on what stands round him. That can wait, though he cannot say why. And he is a man, not old, not a child or a beast. From that fog the prison of the title takes shape.
73593-meteor-strike:
Donald Westlake wrote Meteor Strike, a science fiction tale printed in the November 1961 issue of Amazing Stories, with pictures by Finlay. Its hero, Harvey Ricks, has always bitten off more than he cared to chew, yet always managed to chew and swallow. Now, standing for the first time in the vacuum of space, he wonders if this bite will choke him.

The tale opens with a plain standing order: seven aluminum crates, each a three-foot cube, crated at Los Angeles for the Quartermaster Base circling the Moon. The order runs through the main office of General Transits at Tangiers, out by helicopter, and on to the Tangiers Poe, the port of embarkation. Westlake builds his tale on the dull path of freight in space, and on one man whose job sends him where the cargo goes.
7423-mike:
P. G. Wodehouse's school story opens on an April morning in the Jackson household, where breakfast passes in silence because the cricket season has not begun. Mike Jackson, the cricketing hero of the family, is off to school, and the novel follows him there. Twelve full-page illustrations by T. M. R. Whitwell accompanied the 1909 edition.

At school, Mike finds a friendly native, practices at the nets, revels by night, and earns his chance in the great matches, including a match against the M.C.C. Wodehouse treats school life with the comedy that later made him famous: masters, rows with the town, picnics, and tight corners evaded. It is a boys' book of cricket and high spirits, the first long outing of a Wodehouse hero.
75164-roy-blakeley-s-roundabout-hike:
Roy Blakeley's Roundabout Hike is a boys' scouting novel by Percy Keese Fitzhugh. Grosset and Dunlap issued it in New York in 1927. It bears the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Barbour drew the illustrations, and a map accompanies the tale. The contents list runs to thirty-two chapters. Roy tells the story in his own voice.

Roy begins by calling this hike the craziest yet. His troop mate Pee-wee Harris makes most of the noise. A capsized boat opens the frontispiece scene. Chapters move through Beaver Chasm and a lake trail. A quitter, a stranger, and a reward stir the plot. Honours and awards come near the close. Fitzhugh wrote whole shelves of such troop tales. Tom Slade and Pee-wee Harris had their own series. The books sold scouting as fun with a code.
77916-dora-s-mistake:
Dora's Mistake is a story for the young by the writer called Aloe. Shaw of London put the book out from Paternoster Row. Aloe had writ The Lost Jewel and The Young Pilgrim before this. Twenty-one chapters run from wanting work to a confession. A front picture shows Dora seated near the side table.

The tabernacle, its curtains, and precious things fill the early chapters. Types, preparation, and sacrifices carry the Bible pattern into the tale. Concealment, dead faith and living faith, and leprosy come midway. Naaman, the twins, and the high priest stand in the later list. Birthday gifts, an arrival, and disappointment lead to the confession close. The tale opens as Agnes scolds a boy for carving her desk. A fit of coughing cuts her threat short in that scene. Mrs Temple comes in to ask what the noise means.
78296-old-slowpoke:
Old Slowpoke is a western story by Howard Morgan, the author of Breed of the Wolf. It opens on a lion hunt in the Yargod Hills. Rall Hollidge's dogs have followed a dozen false trails since morning. Business has been poor of late.

The dog of the title is Old Slowpoke, a fat, hybrid hound who trails far behind the pack. As a hunter he is practically useless, and he eats twice as much as any other dog. Yet Hollidge thinks more of him than of all the rest put together. Man and dog are alike: big, slow-moving and ponderous, deliberate in thought and action. And it is true of both that they usually get what they set out to get. The story is a hunting tale with a warm heart, built on that likeness.
78947-the-poems-of-thomas-gordon-hake:
The Poems of Thomas Gordon Hake, chosen by Alice Meynell, was published in London in 1894 by Elkin Mathews and John Lane, with five hundred copies printed for England. A portrait by Dante Gabriel Rossetti fronts the book. Meynell's note ranges over more than fifty years of verse.

She names Madeline, which Rossetti praised in the Academy in 1871, and Parables and Tales, which he treated in the Fortnightly Review in 1873, down to The New Day of 1890. Hake, she says, has a solemn and distinct note, little to be confused with other poets. His verse shows long intent and a calm choice, with feeling that had a past and keeps a future of power.
8042-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Luke addresses his Gospel to Theophilus, promising an orderly account drawn from eyewitnesses so that his reader may know the certainty of what he was taught. The story begins with the priest Zacharias and the births of John the Baptist and Jesus. And it follows Jesus through Galilee with parables found nowhere else: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, and the rich man and Lazarus. It ends with the resurrection appearances and the ascension.

Luke's interests are distinctive: the poor, women, outcasts, and the joy of forgiveness. His Gospel is the longest and most polished of the four, and its Christmas story is the best loved in the world. In the King James Version, its warmth and narrative skill make it a favourite for reading straight through.
8151-miss-merivale-s-mistake:
Mrs Henry Clarke, M. A. , wrote this domestic novel around a startling discovery, a visit to Kentish Town, and the meeting of Tom and Rhoda. Its chapters follow Pauline's diplomacy, apples of Sodom, an invitation, Pauline's suspicions, a confession, and Polly Smith, toward a conclusion that untangles the mistake of the title. An illustration shows Pauline by a window, taking up a photograph frame, a small object that carries much of the plot.

Clarke writes the kind of family story Victorian readers loved: misunderstandings, pride, and affection working themselves out in drawing rooms and country houses. The novel's interest lies in its heroines' judgment and its gentle moral. For readers of old-fashioned domestic fiction, it is a pleasant, well-made example of the genre.
8200-expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-lu:
Alexander Maclaren's first volume of expositions on Luke covers chapters one to twelve, sermon by sermon. His titles follow the Gospel's opening: Elijah Come Again, True Greatness, The Magnificat, Zacharias's Hymn, The Dayspring from on High, Shepherds and Angels. Simeon's Swan-Song, The Boy in the Temple, John the Preacher of Repentance, The Temptation, Preaching at Nazareth, and A Sabbath in Capernaum. Each exposition takes one passage and draws out its devotional meaning.

Maclaren preaches Luke as the Gospel of grace for outsiders, and his sermons suit both preachers and private readers. The volume's steady pace lets a reader work through Luke's infancy and early ministry with a trusted guide. It remains a clear, warm example of Victorian expository preaching.
8269-the-world-english-bible-web-luke:
Luke is the longest Gospel, written in polished Greek by a careful storyteller who says he checked his sources. It alone tells of shepherds at the manger, the boy Jesus in the temple, and the parables of the good Samaritan and the prodigal son. Women, outcasts, and the poor stand near the center of the story throughout, and meals shared with strangers recur like a refrain.

From the birth stories in Bethlehem to the road to Emmaus after the resurrection, Luke stresses mercy and joy. Its second volume, Acts, continues the story into the early church. Readers who want the fullest, most humane portrait of Jesus in the Gospels usually start here.
868-the-philosopher-s-joke:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this short tale that opens with the narrator's frank doubt: he does not believe the story himself. Six persons, he says, are persuaded of its truth, and their hope is to convince themselves and others that a philosopher's joke can carry real weight. The joke itself turns on a trick of thought.

Jerome lets the tale hover between jest and earnest, with his usual light touch. The fun lies in watching sober folk defend an absurdity, and in the narrator's refusal to join them. The piece is brief and witty, a small example of Jerome's gift for turning a parlour paradox into a story.
8830-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Luke's gospel, in Weymouth's modern speech, opens as a historian's letter: many have attempted a narrative of facts received with full assurance. On the authority of eyewitnesses devoted to the divine message. Luke, after careful investigation from the commencement, writes a connected account for most noble Theophilus. He may fully know the truth of things taught by word of mouth. Zechariah, priest in Herod's time, and his wife follow.

From that orderly beginning, Luke tells the births of John and Jesus, the ministry of compassion, parables found nowhere else. The journey to Jerusalem, in the longest gospel's humane voice. Weymouth's version keeps Luke's careful sentences readable without losing their warmth. Readers who want the gospel of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son in plain English will find this volume a clear, complete Luke.
blackbeard-or-the-pirate-of-roanoke:
B. Barker published this tale of the Atlantic with F. Gleason of Boston in 1847, at the Flag of Our Union office. Barker, author of The Sea Serpent and Dwarf of the Channel, opens on Trinidad, two hundred leagues from Brazil. The Earl of Derwentwater's party lands amid enchanted scenery and unnatural sounds. Then the notorious pirate Blackbeard suddenly appears.

A heroine's forced marriage drives the Gothic machinery. Clarice faces dread alternatives: death for her father and herself, or the sacrifice forever of her happiness and peace of mind. In her terror she chooses the latter, and that night she is united to Rowland by her own priest, compelled to officiate. Her father must will all his vast riches to his murderous son-in-law. Barker's Blackbeard is the penny-dreadful villain of legend, not the historical Teach.
britannica-1911-albert-archduke:
Albert, Archduke of Austria, a field-marshal of 1817 to 1895, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Eldest son of the archduke Charles, he was born at Vienna in August 1817 and educated under his father's careful eye. He entered the Austrian army as a colonel of infantry in 1837.
