Cavalry service, a brigade at Graz, and high command in Upper and Lower Austria followed.

Albert worked hard to keep his troops efficient while most European armies sank to a low level, learning troop-leading from Radetzky in Italy. When war came in 1866 he took command of the field army in Italy. With greatly inferior forces he won the brilliant victory of Custozza in June of that year. Eight days of field operations fixed his reputation as a general-in-chief. He married Princess Hildegarde of Bavaria in 1844, a personal detail the entry records among the commands.
britannica-1911-angell-george-thorndike:
Kindness to animals, not law, made George Thorndike Angell (1823–1909) known. Born at Southbridge, Massachusetts, on 5 June 1823, he took his degree at Dartmouth in 1846, read law at Harvard Law School, and joined the Boston bar in 1851. He practised there many years. His public work began in earnest in 1868.

That year Angell founded the Massachusetts Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals and took its presidency. He also launched a journal, Our Dumb Animals, to spread humane treatment. He helped set up humane societies in England and America, started the Bands of Mercy movement in 1882, and founded the American Humane Education Society in 1889. Criminology and fights for pure-food and public-health laws added to his name. He died at Boston on 16 March 1909.
britannica-1911-archduke:
Archduke is a title peculiar to Austria's royal family. Its Latin form is archidux. German uses Erzherzog for it. Selden said it denotes pre-eminence only. It grants no power over other dukes, he argued. Archbishop differs in conveying real superiority. Bruno of Saxony perhaps assumed it in the stronger sense. He divided Lorraine into two dukedoms then. That was in the tenth century.

The designation stayed exceedingly rare in medieval times. Lorraine's archduke title died with its circumstances. Brabant's later dynasties bore only duke. Habsburg did not inherit the title from Lorraine. Imperial charters to Austria never grant it. Abbot Rudolph mentions an Archidux Austriae rhetorically. His chronicle dates to the twelfth century. The entry traces the title's forged privileges carefully. Huber and Erben anchor its documentary scholarship.
britannica-1911-artichoke:
The common artichoke is a plant of the daisy order with some likeness to a large thistle. It has long been prized as a food plant for the table. The parts men eat are the young heart of the flower head and the base of the scales round it, known as artichoke bottoms.

In Italy those hearts, dried, go much into soups, the 1911 Britannica entry says. It then parts off a namesake plant, the Jerusalem artichoke, a kin plant grown for its tubers. That plant is much like a sunflower, and its odd name is a garble of an Italian phrase for it. It came from the north east of America, where the first folk grew it. Its tubers are rich in a plant starch and in sugar.
britannica-1911-basingstoke:
Basingstoke, a market town and municipal borough in Hampshire, England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as standing forty-eight miles west-south-west of London, served by two railways. Its population in 1901 was 9793. St Michael and All Angels is praised as a fine late Perpendicular building, mostly of Henry VIII's time. The ruined Holy Ghost chapel, in an ancient cemetery, was built for a local guild founded in 1525.

History runs deep around the town. Nearby Old Basing holds the remains of Basing House, famous for the fifth marquess of Winchester's stubborn resistance to Cromwell before its fall in 1645 after a long siege. Excavations showed Roman occupation, and the first recorded event is a victory by Æthelred and Alfred over the Danes in 871. The town traded in farm goods, brewing, farm implements, and clothing. Its canal to the Wey had lost trade to the railways.
britannica-1911-brown-henry-kirke:
Henry Kirke Brown, an American sculptor, was born in Massachusetts in eighteen fourteen. He began to paint portraits while still quite a boy at home. He studied painting in Boston and learned a little of modelling there. In the late eighteen thirties he worked summers as a railroad engineer. That work earned the means for him to study further in his art.

Brown spent four years in Italy, from eighteen forty two to eighteen forty six. On his return to New York he stayed distinctively American in style. Italian influence never ruled him as it ruled so many early American sculptors. His horse statues are excellent, above all those of Scott and of Washington. The Washington statue of eighteen fifty six was the second such work made in America. Brown was among the first in America to cast his own bronzes.
britannica-1911-carisbrooke:
Carisbrooke is a town in the Isle of Wight, England. It stands one mile south of Newport. Its population in 1901 was 3993. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its castle and history. The Lugley brook valley parts the village from a steep hill. That conical hill is crowned by Carisbrooke castle. Roman villa remains lie in the valley.

No reliable mention of Carisbrooke survives from Saxon times. The Domesday Survey does not name the town itself. Its manor of Bowcombe was a royal dependency then. William Fitz Osbern gained it from the king in exchange. He probably raised the castle, and became first lord of the island. Lordship of the Isle of Wight stayed tied to the castle. Henry I gave it to Richard de Redvers. Isabella de Fortibus later sold it to Edward I. A pentagonal fort guarded it against the Armada threat.
britannica-1911-coke:
Coke is the product left when coal is heated hard out of touch with air. The heat drives off the parts that can pass into gas. What stays is mostly carbon, the fixed carbon of the coal. Ash from the coal stays in it as well. Small shares of hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen remain, no more than two or three per cent in all.

Heat and speed shape the result. Fast, low heat, as in gas making, gives a dull black, spongy coke. It lights with ease and suits open grates. Long, hard heat gives a dense coke with a bright, half-metal sheen. That kind serves iron and steel melting. Long later sections treat ovens and methods in fine detail. Stamping gear and moulding boxes get close attention. The entry closes with a list of papers on oven types.
britannica-1911-constable-sir-marmaduke:
Marmaduke Constable, who lived from about 1455 to 1518, was an English soldier. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his house and kin. His family took its name from ties to the constables of Chester. He was a son of Robert Constable of Flamborough.

Constable campaigned in France under two English kings. He served as sheriff in Staffordshire and in Yorkshire. Both Henry the Seventh and Henry the Eighth held him in favor. In 1513 he led his kin and men to the battle of Flodden. A rhymed stone in Flamborough church still tells his deeds. The entry then follows his sons, one hanged for treason in 1537. A later kinsman sat in judgment on King Charles the First.
britannica-1911-erie-lake:
Erie is the most southerly of the Great Lakes of North America, lying between Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New York to the south and Ontario to the north. It is nearly elliptical, its long axis of 250 miles running east and west. Its greatest breadth is 60 miles, and its area about 10,000 square miles. Its surface stands 573 feet above sea level, about 9 feet below Lake Huron and 327 feet above Lake Ontario.

Lake Erie is very shallow, and the entry divides it into three basins. The western basin has a flat bottom at 5 to 6 fathoms. The main basin deepens gently to 14 fathoms, and the eastern part holds a hollow 30 fathoms deep. The flat soil on its shores is very fertile, and peaches, grapes, and small fruits are widely grown. Because the lake is shallow, storms stir it easily, making navigation rough and dangerous.
britannica-1911-fildes-sir-luke:
Sir Luke Fildes is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Fildes was an English painter, born at Liverpool in 1844. He trained at the South Kensington and Royal Academy schools. He first won success as an illustrator of high rank.

Later he took his place among the ablest English painters of his day. The entry names the works that made that name. The Casual Ward came in 1874 and The Widower in 1876. The Village Wedding followed in 1883, and The Doctor in 1891. That last picture hangs in the National Gallery of British Art. Fildes also painted scenes of Venetian life and many portraits. Among them were the coronation portraits of King Edward the Seventh and Queen Alexandra. He was knighted in 1906, and the article closes with a guide to his biography.
britannica-1911-fluke:
Fluke, probably linked with the German flach, flat, is a name spread across several flat things. It is given to flat fish, above all the common flounder. It also names a trematode worm, flounder-shaped, that lives as a parasite in the liver and nearby organs of animals, especially sheep, and causes liver-rot. The commonest is Fasciola hepatica. Fluke is also the name of a species of kidney potato grown for the table.

From likeness to the fish's shape, fluke names the triangular holding-plates at the ends of an anchor's arms. It also names the triangular ends of a whale's tail, the flukes that drive it through the water. Last, the word serves in slang for a lucky accident. That use, the entry says, seems to have begun in billiards, where a fluke was a scoring shot the player never meant to make.
britannica-1911-graham-s-dyke:
Graham's Dyke is an antiquities article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Roman frontier wall across the narrow waist of Scotland. The dyke, also called a sheugh or trench, ran from the Forth to the Clyde, about 36 miles. From about the year 140 to about 185 it formed the northern frontier of Roman Britain. Antiquaries more often call it the Wall of Pius or the Antonine Vallum, after the emperor Antoninus Pius, in whose reign it was raised.

The article is chiefly a study of the strange local name. The oldest spelling, Grymisdyke in Fordun in 1385, shows the name is the same as Grim's Ditch, found in England for other early ramparts. Grim, the article explains, seems to be a Teutonic god or devil to whom men credited earthworks thrown up in impossibly short times.
britannica-1911-grand-duke:
Grand-duke is a title article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a rank held by princes between king and duke. The dignity was first granted in 1567 by Pope Pius the Fifth to Cosimo the First. In 1806 Napoleon made his brother in law Joachim Murat grand-duke of Berg, and the rulers of Hesse-Darmstadt and Baden took the title on joining the Confederation of the Rhine.

By the rulings of the Congress of Vienna the title passed to the sovereigns of Luxemburg, Saxony, the two Mecklenburgs, and Oldenburg. The emperors of Austria and the kings of Prussia hold it among their lesser styles. In Russia, grand-duke renders veliky knyaz, more truly grand-prince. That was once the title of the overlord of the house of Rurik. The right to grant it later sat with the Tatar Khan, who gave it to the prince of Moscow.
britannica-1911-great-bear-lake: Great Bear Lake is a large fresh water lake in the north west of Canada. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes a sheet of very uneven shape between 65 and 67 degrees north. Its area is put at about eleven thousand square miles, with a depth of 270 feet. The Great Bear river carries its waters into the Mackenzie river. Fish fill the lake in plenty. The land around it is barren and bare of crops, yet it holds much game for hunters.
britannica-1911-greville-charles-cavendi:
Charles Cavendish Fulke Greville (1794-1865) was an English diarist, born on 2 April 1794, great-grandson of the 5th earl of Warwick. The 1911 Britannica entry has him a page of George III, educated at Eton and Christ Church. He left Oxford early, made private secretary to Earl Bathurst before he was twenty.

Family interest gave him sinecures, and in 1821 he became clerk of the council in ordinary. He held the post nearly forty years, serving George IV, William IV and Victoria. The office carried no political duties, the entry notes, but it brought him into daily contact with the chiefs of every party. Well-born, handsome and accomplished, he lived the easy life of a man of fashion. His lasting work is the diary he kept through those decades, a private record of the court and politics of his age.
britannica-1911-hake:
The hake is the subject of a fish entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It differs from the cod in having only two dorsal fins and one anal fin. It is very common on the coasts of Europe and eastern North America. Its flesh is much less esteemed than that of the true cod family.

Specimens four feet in length are not scarce, the entry notes. Local uses of the name hake vary from place to place. In America the silver hake, sometimes called whiting, is also a food fish. A Pacific kind is named as well. Both American kinds are rated as food of lower quality.
britannica-1911-hansard-luke:
Luke Hansard (1752–1828) was an English printer. He was born in Norwich on 5 July 1752. Boston grammar school educated him. A Norwich printer took him as apprentice. He reached London with only a guinea in his pocket. John Hughs, printer to the House of Commons, employed him. In 1774 Hansard became a partner there. By 1800 the business was wholly his.

He printed the Journals of the House of Commons from 1774 until death. Pitt once got a secret report's proofs within twenty-four hours. That promptitude repeatedly served the government. Burke, Johnson and Orme were among his friends. Porson called him the most accurate printer of Greek. The 1801 union with Ireland swelled parliamentary printing hugely. Hansard gave up nearly all private work in response. He devised many ways to cut the reports' costs. His firm became Luke Hansard & Sons.
britannica-1911-holyoke:
Holyoke is a city of Hampden county, Massachusetts, in a bend of the Connecticut river, about 8 m. N. of Springfield. Its people numbered 21,915 in 1880, 45,712 in 1900 and 57,730 in 1910. In 1900 nearly 19,000 were foreign-born, French-Canadians and Irish the largest groups. Two railways and an interurban line serve the city, whose area is about 17 square miles.

Above the city the Connecticut falls some 60 ft. through the rift between Mt Tom and Mt Holyoke. That water-power lay unused until 1849, when a dam 1,017 ft. long was finished and canals were laid out to use it. The work turned a farming village into a great manufacturing centre, ninth in the commonwealth by 1900. A stone dam of 1900, 1,020 ft. long, cost about $750,000. Cotton goods came first in its trade, and later paper products, in which Holyoke now leads all cities. The city is also the station for Mt Holyoke College at South Hadley.
britannica-1911-hullah-john-pyke:
English composer and music teacher John Pyke Hullah, born at Worcester in eighteen twelve, is given a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a pupil of William Horsley from eighteen twenty nine. He entered the Royal Academy of Music in eighteen thirty three.

He wrote an opera to words by Dickens, staged in eighteen thirty six. Two more operas followed at Covent Garden. In eighteen thirty nine he went to Paris to study how music was taught to large groups. He took up a fixed note system, and his version was taught with great success for twenty years. A large hall built for him in London was lost to fire in eighteen sixty.
britannica-1911-luke:
Luke is held to be the author of the third Gospel and of the Book of Acts. He is the most literary of the writers of the New Testament. He alone of them was not of Jewish birth, a fact of great weight for his works. His name is a short, familiar form of Lucanus. His trade was that of a physician, as Paul notes in a letter.

Those two facts hint that Luke was the son of a Greek freedman, perhaps tied to Lucania in south Italy. Since Caesar gave Roman civic rights to all physicians in Rome, Luke may have gained that rank from his father. In any case, such a man would hold the view of things Roman that his works show. He worked with Paul in Rome. He seems to have stayed close by his leader there, as doctor and as aide.
britannica-1911-mameluke: Mameluke is a very short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word came into English through French from the Arabic mamluk, meaning a slave. It is the name given to a line of Egyptian sultans. Their rule began in 1250, when the bodyguard of Turkish slaves, first formed in Egypt under the successors of Saladin, seized supreme power for itself. The article is only a definition and a date, with a cross-reference to the history of Egypt.
britannica-1911-maracaibo-lake:
Maracaibo is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a large lake in western Venezuela. The lake stretches southward from the Gulf of Venezuela. It opens into that gulf through a long neck, or strait, blocked at its mouth by islands and bars. Its wide drainage basin is bounded by ranges of mountains on three sides.

The lake is roughly four sided in shape, the entry says. Inside the bar the water is about thirty feet deep, and the lake can bear vessels of large size. Many rivers feed it, chiefly on its west and south sides. The largest of them are named in turn, and the first three have channels fit for river steamers. A number of small lakes lie near the main lake's southern and western shores, the article adds.
britannica-1911-marston-philip-bourke:
Philip Bourke Marston, a blind English poet, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in 1850, he was a playwright's son of note. His father John Westland Marston kept verse drama on the stage. Dickens, Macready, and Kean were friends at that family table. The boy grew up in a house steeped in books and plays.

Great names of the age crossed that Chalk Farm door in his youth. The Rossettis and Swinburne came among that bright young set. From his fourth year his sight failed by slow degrees. An accident helped that loss till he was near blind in full. Death took his mother, his bride to be, and kin in turn. His sister wrote down his verse till death took her too.
britannica-1911-mohonk-lake:
Mohonk Lake is a summer settlement in Ulster county, New York, described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It sits at the north end of the lake of the same name. The lake is a small body of water set high on Sky Top Mountain. That peak is one of the highest of the Shawangunk range.

The rise of the place as a resort is credited to Albert Keith Smiley. He was a graduate of Haverford College who ran schools in several states. In eighteen sixty nine he bought land at the lake's north end and built a large hotel. There, in eighteen eighty three, the first conference of friends of the American Indian met. Those meetings have been held each year since, with a wider scope from nineteen oh four.
britannica-1911-mortlake: Mortlake is a town in Surrey in England, on the Thames west of London. Its parish held just past seven thousand folk in nineteen one. The town is known as the end point of the great boat race of two famed schools since eighteen forty-five. Its manor was held by church heads till the days of Henry the Eighth, then passed to the Crown. In past days it was famed for woven hang art.
britannica-1911-ontario-lake:
Ontario, Lake, the least and most east of the Great Lakes, is mapped in words in the 1911 Britannica. It lies between the province of Ontario and the state of New York. Its long axis runs east and west for one hundred eighty miles. Its water face spans more than seven thousand square miles. Its great depth tops seven hundred feet in the deep part.

North shores rise in a soft grade to broad farm plains. South shores hold a ridge set back from the lake for miles. Fruit farms and grape rows crowd the low strip by that ridge. The Niagara River is its chief feed stream of all. Fruit lands by the Bay of Quinte close the rich shore list. Its out flow at Kingston feeds the Saint Lawrence River.
britannica-1911-pasquier-etienne-denis-d:
Etienne Denis Pasquier, a French statesman born in seventeen sixty seven, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in April of that year, he came from a family long famed at the bar and in the high courts of France. He was bred for the law and schooled at the college of Juilly.

He then rose to a post in the high court of Paris. From that seat he watched the clash grow between that court and Louis the Sixteenth. Those were the years just before the great change of seventeen eighty nine broke out. His own views were those of a mild man for reform. He wished to renew the old order, not to end it. His life notes set that court in a kind light. The entry gives a calm insider view of a court on the edge of a storm.
britannica-1911-paulding-james-kirke:
James Kirke Paulding is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Paulding was an American writer and statesman who lived from 1778 to 1860. He was born in Dutchess County in New York. After brief village schooling he moved to New York City in 1800. With Washington Irving and a kinsman he began a set of light humorous pieces in 1807.

The article tells how a political pamphlet won him notice from President Madison. He served on the board of navy commissioners and as navy agent in New York. From 1837 to 1841 he was secretary of the navy under President Van Buren. He wrote essays, poems, and tales in large number. He held strong anti British views from his father's example. He was among the first writers to insist on a truly American voice in letters.
britannica-1911-peruke: Peruke is an old word for a wig, an artificial head of hair, says a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The word comes from a French form, itself taken from an Italian term. That term is most often linked to a word for hair. In the sixteen hundreds the French word took many English forms. Those forms were worn down step by step into periwig, and then into wig. Periwig is at times kept for the heavy full wigs worn under Charles the Second.
britannica-1911-rawlinson-sir-henry-cres:
Sir Henry Creswicke Rawlinson (1810-1895), an English soldier and student of the East, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Oxfordshire, he went to India in 1827 as a cadet of the East India Company. After six years with his regiment, in which he mastered Persian, he was sent to Persia with other English officers to drill the Shah's troops.

The article says that work first drew him to old inscriptions, above all those in the cuneiform script, which no one could yet read. For two years he lived near the great rock inscription at Behistun and copied as much of it as he could. Strife between the courts sent the English officers home. In 1840 he became the political agent at Kandahar, where his work and his bravery in the Afghan War won him high praise.
britannica-1911-sake: Saké is a short drink note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the national beverage of Japan. Made chiefly from rice, it stands midway between beer and wine, with 12 to 15 per cent of alcohol. Some 20,000 breweries in Japan turn out about 150 million gallons a year. The liquor is yellowish white, tasting somewhat like madeira or sherry, and is drunk warmed. The name is said to come from Osaka, a town long famed for its saké.
britannica-1911-scone-cake: Scone is a short food entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a Scots cake. A scone is made of wheat or barley meal and baked on a griddle. The cakes are round and are most often cut into four parts, giving a wedge shape with a curved edge. The broad lowland bonnet was called a scone cap from the same shape. The word seems to be a short form of a Low German term, Schonbrot, meaning fine bread.
britannica-1911-shrike:
Shrike, a bird's name, is traced in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Turner gave the name in 1544, but only on the word of Sir Francis Lovell. He had seen the bird twice in England, yet found no one else who called it so. Later writers took the word up anyway. Butcher-bird stayed its common name in speech.

In books it kept first place in literary English. It was then widely extended to all birds of the shrike family and others besides. The Latin name Lanius began with Gesner in 1555. He thought the birds he named had not been mentioned by the ancients. The shrike Turner meant is the great grey shrike, also called the greater butcher-bird. It visits the British Islands fairly regularly in autumn or winter, though in small numbers. It sometimes stays into the next summer, but has never been proved to breed there.
britannica-1911-smoke:
Smoke is defined in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as the vapour that flees from a burning thing. The stress falls on the seen cloud from coal, wood, peat, and plant stuff. The entry treats not the science of smoke in the large. It treats the laws and steps used to curb the harm of too much smoke.

Harm from coal smoke was known in London at an early date. In thirteen hundred and six a man was put to death for burning sea coal in the city. Yet the text says the theme drew real weight only in modern times. A first smoke curb tool is dated to seventeen eighty five. Readers who need the past of clean air law in Britain will find a firm, dated start here.
britannica-1911-sticke:
Sticke is a games article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a court game that grew out of lawn tennis. Its name comes from sphairistike, the parent game. Play uses a plain lawn-tennis racket and balls with no flannel cover. The court is walled in, with walls of wood, cement, or brick nine or ten feet high and netting above.

The court itself is seventy-eight feet long and twenty-seven feet wide. A painted line splits it lengthwise, and a net three feet six inches high splits it across. In each corner a nine-foot square marks the service court, and service lines are drawn eighteen feet from each back wall. The rules match those of lawn tennis save for one point. A ball counts as out only if struck over the walls.
britannica-1911-sunstroke:
Sunstroke is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an illness from heat. The text gives heatstroke, insolation, and thermic fever as like names. The term names harm done to the central nervous system. That harm spreads through the nerves to other organs. It comes from exposure to the sun or to hot air. The ailment is most often seen in tropical lands. It also strikes in temperate lands in hot weather.

Moist air makes the danger much worse for the body. Damp air blocks the cooling of an overheated frame. The ailment was chiefly studied among soldiers in India. There it once formed a large share of sickness and death. Army heads later gave more care to health and comfort. Barracks and dress drew fresh attention from them. The timing and mode of troop moves were also set with care. Those steps cut the toll of the disease.
britannica-1911-superior-lake:
Lake Superior is the most north western of the Great Lakes of North America. Its lake entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the largest body of fresh water in the world by area. Ontario bounds it east and north, and three states bound it south.

The lake holds deep, cold, and clear water along rocky high shores. Its form is a wide crescent that bends toward the north side. It runs about three hundred eighty three miles long on its curve. Its greatest breadth is one hundred sixty miles, and depth tops a thousand feet. Two hundred rivers feed it, and its basin drains a vast land.
britannica-1911-tuke:
Tuke is the name of an English house whose men of four ages won fame for good works for their fellow men. William Tuke, born at York in seventeen thirty-two, is linked to kind care of the mad. He set up a home at York in seventeen ninety-two where the mad were led with no harsh bonds.

His son helped that work and writ books on morals and faith. The next in line spread word of that York home in a famed book and pled for kind homes for the poor mad. The last named is recalled for aid work in Ireland in its hard years.
britannica-1911-wake:
Wake is a custom article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word now names the Irish custom of watching all night by a corpse before burial. Its older sense was wider: a vigil kept each year by a parish church. That feast marked the building or dedication of the church.

The entry describes the old church wake in detail. The night was spent in prayer and meditation inside the church. Tents and booths rose in the churchyard before dawn. The next day was a holiday of feasting, dancing, and sports. People from nearby parishes travelled in to join the fun. In time the wakes slid into mere fairs and merry-making. Complaints about that slide reach back to the reign of King Edgar. The article follows a holy watch as it turned into a village holiday.
burke:
John Morley wrote a life of Edmund Burke for the English Men of Letters series, in a library print of 1907. First print came in 1888, with fresh runs in 1892, 1897, and 1902. A note at the front owns the book's mixed roots. Three pages come from Morley's Britannica piece on Burke.

Twenty years past, Morley had put out a Burke study of pure critique, with no tale of the life. Score of pages from that book live on here at most. The rest is new work, life-led rather than fault-led, by his own account. A Greek rule fronts his plea: a man may say a thing once as he would have it said, and hardly twice. Burke the speaker, thinker, and statesman fills the frame that plea defends.
by-pike-and-dyke:
G. A. Henty wrote a boys' tale of the Dutch rise against Spain, in a text dated 1889. A letter to his dear lads fronts the book. No fight in all past time, he holds, was so lopsided, so long held, and so hard pressed as this one. Fishers, sailors, and farm folk stood on one side.

Spain, the great power of the age, stood on the other. A bigot king drove it, set to force his faith on the Dutch or wipe them out, by Henty's charge. One prince, stout hearts, a just cause, and the sea as sole friend held the Dutch line. Pike and dyke — spear and sea wall — name the twin tools of that stand in the title. Faith and freedom form the stakes, with the faith named first by the author's own hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnes-mary-cl:
Agnes Mary Clerke was an astronomer born at Skibbereen, County Cork, on 10 February 1842. She died in London on 20 January 1907. She showed marked interest in astronomy from the start of her study. Before fifteen she had begun writing that science's history. Dublin took the family in 1861, Queenstown in 1863. Later she went to Italy, staying chiefly at Florence until 1877, studying at the public library.

London became her home in 1877. Her first important article, Copernicus in Italy, appeared in the Edinburgh Review that October. She won world-wide reputation in 1885 with A Popular History of Astronomy in the Nineteenth Century, at once recognized as authoritative. Though not a practical astronomer, she passed three months at the Cape Observatory in 1888 as Sir David Gill's guest, gaining familiarity with spectroscopic work. In 1892 the Royal Institution awarded her its Actonian Prize of one hundred guineas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-larke:
Blessed John Larke, an English martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. He died at Tyburn on 7 March 1544 after a long parish career: rector of St. Ethelburga's, Bishopsgate, from 1505, of Woodford from 1527, and of Chelsea from 1530, on Thomas More's presentation. More's parish priest and personal friend, he is styled doctor, though his faculty is unknown.

Indicted in February 1544 with German Gardiner, John Ireland, and John Heywood, he was condemned for denying the royal supremacy. Heywood recanted on the hurdle and lived, while Larke, Gardiner, and Ireland suffered together at Tyburn, their heads and quarters buried under the gallows. The entry presents a parish priest caught in Henry's last terror.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-burke:
Edmund Burke was the first Vicar Apostolic of Nova Scotia, born in County Kildare in 1753 and dead at Halifax in 1820. Barred from study at home by the penal laws, he trained in Paris, then sailed to Canada in 1786 and taught philosophy and mathematics at the Quebec seminary. He longed for mission work, and in 1794 he was sent to Upper Canada.

For seven years he rode a hard pioneer circuit among scattered Catholics, and he spoke plainly about race prejudice hurting the faith. Sent to Halifax in 1801, he became Vicar-General of Nova Scotia in 1815 and Bishop of Zion in 1818. The entry credits him with steady work for faith, schooling, and civic life in the early years of the province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ellen-mary-cl:
Ellen Mary Clerke was an Irish journalist and novelist, sister of Agnes Mary Clerke, born at Skibbereen in 1840 and dead in London in 1906. A gifted writer, she served for many years as an editorial writer for the London Tablet. She had a striking grasp of the religious and political tangles of continental Europe. Seven years in Italy made her at home in its language, literature, and public life.

She sent Florence periodicals a series of stories perfect in Italian phrase, idiom, and local colour. Her pamphlets Jupiter and His System and The Planet Venus added to popular astronomy. In 1899 she published Fable and Song in Italy. It holds essays and studies with Italian poems turned into English in their original metres. Her last work was the novel Flowers of Fire, issued in 1902.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-sai:
The Gospel of Saint Luke opens with a biography of Saint Luke, probably an abbreviation of Lucanus, generally held a native of Antioch. Eusebius calls him a physician who lived long and closely with Paul and knew the other apostles well. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats the Gospel's authenticity, integrity, purpose, contents, sources, and accuracy.

The article also takes up disputed points: Lysanias, Tetrarch of Abilene, who spoke the Magnificat, the census of Quirinius, and Luke's relation to Josephus. The writer's special interest in Antioch and acquaintance with it appear in Acts, where the city recurs again and again. Luke's name itself seems unknown before the Christian Era, though Lucanus is common in inscriptions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-von-:
Medieval poet Heinrich von Veldeke, a knight born near Maastricht about the middle of the twelfth century, pioneered courtly romance in Germany. Learned in Latin and French and familiar with Virgil and Ovid, he first wrote a legend of St. Servatius for a Countess of Looz, then turned to his great Eneide on Aeneas and Dido.

Most of the Eneide was done by 1175 at Cleves when its manuscript, lent to a countess, was carried to Thuringia. After nine years he recovered and finished it under Hermann of Saxony before 1190. Based on an old French romance and thoroughly medievalized around love, it fixed the short rhyming couplet, strict metre, pure rhyme, and courtly style that later epic writers followed. His lyrics brought French forms into Minnesong.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-lemcke:
Henry Lemcke, a missionary in the United States, was born at Rhena in Mecklenburg in 1796, converted from Protestant preaching to Catholicism in 1824, and was ordained at Ratisbon in 1826. Coming to America in 1834, he served briefly at Holy Trinity in Philadelphia, then assisted the aged Prince Gallitzin at Loretto, Pennsylvania, from Ebensburg, covering some fifty miles. In 1838 he laid out Carrolltown, named for John Carroll, the United States' first Catholic bishop, succeeding Gallitzin at Loretto in 1840.

Lemcke brought the first Benedictines to America under Boniface Wimmer, future archabbot of St. Vincent's, and joined the new community himself in 1852. In 1855 he travelled as missionary to Kansas, opening the way for St. Benedict's Abbey at Atchison, then served at Elizabeth, New Jersey, from 1861 to 1877, spending his remaining years at Carrolltown, where he died in 1882. He also wrote a life of Prince Gallitzin, published at Münster in 1861.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-ernst-ja:
Karl Ernst Jarcke was born at Danzig in 1801, of a Protestant merchant family, and died at Vienna in 1852. He studied jurisprudence and taught criminal law at Bonn and later at Berlin. His Handbuch des gemeinen deutschen Strafrechts appeared in three volumes from 1827 to 1830. Longing for faith, he became a Catholic at Cologne in 1824.

His anonymous brochure on the French Revolution of 1830 won the approval of the crown prince's anti-revolutionary circle. He edited their Politische Wochenblatt from 1831, and Metternich called him to Vienna's State Chancery in 1832. In 1837 he parted from his Berlin friends over the Cologne Occurrence, the archbishop's imprisonment, which they approved and he condemned. His ideal was the medieval Germanic state, with a hereditary monarch and a state confined to war and justice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-proske:
Karl Proske was born at Grobing in Upper Silesia in 1794 and died in 1861. After a Halle medical doctorate he became court physician at Oppeln and served as an army surgeon in 1813 to 1815. He also loved ecclesiastical chant with enthusiasm. In 1821 he resolved on the priesthood, and Ratisbon ordained him in April 1826.

From then on he gave himself to ancient church music, spending his income and preferments on searching Italian and other archives. In 1830 he became canon and Kapellmeister of Ratisbon cathedral, where he had sung as vicar choral since 1827. Patiently he gathered and copied hundreds of musical scores. In 1853 he began his Musica Divina, whose fourth volume appeared in 1862, followed by his two-volume Selectus Novus Missarum of 1857 to 1861.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luke-joseph-h:
Luke Joseph Hooke was an Irish theologian at the Sorbonne, born at Dublin in 1716 and dead at St. Cloud in 1796. Son of historian Nathaniel Hooke, he was schooled at Paris under penal laws that barred Catholic learning in Ireland, took his licentiate, and graduated at the Sorbonne in 1736.

Given a theology chair in 1742, he won a name for learning, then stumbled over de Prades's thesis in 1751. Admitting he had not read it, he withdrew his signature and sought condemnation, yet the faculty censured all three signatories and Cardinal de Tencin stripped him of his chair in 1752. Restored in part, he later held Hebrew, curated the Mazarin library, and lost that post in 1791 for refusing the clergy oath.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-locke:
Exeter-born composer Matthew Locke (1629-1677) sang as a boy chorister at Exeter Cathedral and built a career in Restoration theatre and court music. He shared in Shirley's masque Cupid and Death in 1653, became a Catholic in 1654, and wrote music for Davenant's Siege of Rhodes in 1656. In 1661 he scored the procession march for Charles II's crowning and joined the king's private band.

Later work includes incidental music for the Dryden-Davenant Tempest of 1667, the theory book Melothesia of 1673, music for Shadwell's Psyche, and anthems and Latin hymns. The famous Macbeth score long tied to his name was almost surely Purcell's, written for a 1689 revival. Locke also fought a sharp pamphlet war with Thomas Salmon over writing all music on one clef, and his side won.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-henry:
Patrick Henry O'Rorke was an American soldier born in County Cavan on 25 March 1837 and killed at Gettysburg in July 1863. A year old when his parents emigrated, he grew up in Rochester, New York, attended public schools, and worked as a marble-cutter from 1853. Soon after he won a West Point cadetship and graduated with highest honours in June 1861.

Commissioned a regular lieutenant, he served with distinction as an engineer staff officer, then became colonel of the 140th New York Volunteers, fighting at Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville. At Gettysburg, defending Little Round Top at the battle's crisis, he seized the colours, climbed a rock to rally his men, and fell dead. The Comte de Paris called it one of the battle's most striking and dramatic scenes. His widow became a Sacred Heart religious and educator.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-majunke:
Paul Majunke was a German Catholic journalist born at Gross-Schmograu in Silesia on 14 July 1842 and dead at Hochkirch near Glogau on 21 May 1899. He entered Breslau University in 1861 for four years of civil and canon law and Catholic theology, was ordained in 1867, and edited the Koelnische Zeitung from 1869 to 1870. From 1871 to 1878 he edited Germania as chief, and in 1874 won election to the Reichstag, joining the Centre party, with a Prussian deputies' seat in 1878.

During the Kulturkampf he championed Catholic causes with zeal and fearlessness at great personal cost. Uncompromising zeal, however, drove him to ill-timed words in press and parliament that estranged leading Catholics. In 1874 he drew a year's imprisonment for press-law breaches, and even a Reichstag motion failed to remit it. From 1878 to 1884 he edited the Centre papers' correspondence, and as Hochkirch parish priest from 1884 he kept writing, above all his History of the Kulturkampf.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pembroke:
Pembroke was a Canadian diocese centred on a lumber and farming town on the Ottawa River. About a hundred miles west of Ottawa, the town grew from early Indian missions, where Sulpicians Dupins and Bellefeuille preached in 1836 and Father Gillie built the first church in 1847. That church, enlarged in stone, became the Cathedral of St. Columba when the district gained its own bishop.

The territory was cut from Ottawa, Three Rivers, and St. Boniface and set up as the Vicariate of Pontiac in 1882, reaching north toward Hudson Bay. Rapid settlement and the gold and silver finds of the Cobalt region led to its erection as the Diocese of Pembroke in 1898. A new vicariate at Timiskaming followed in 1908. Narcisse Zéphyrin Lorrain was its first bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-aske:
Robert Aske fronted a rising of 30,000 northern Catholics in 1536 against Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries. An English gentleman, he headed a movement with sweeping demands. It sought the suppression of Lutheran books and the punishment of heretical bishops and evil royal advisers. It also sought the recall of anti-church laws, prosecution of the king's visitors Lee and Layton, and a parliament in the North.

Alarmed at the rising's size, Henry offered a full pardon and promised redress at a parliament at York. Aske then disbanded his army. When the king broke his promises, the insurgents took the field again, only to be beaten by the Duke of Norfolk in attempts on Hull and Carlisle. Most leaders were hanged by scores. Aske himself was executed at York in June 1537.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-bicker:
Robert Bickerdike was a Yorkshire layman martyred at York in 1585 for small acts of Catholic loyalty. Living at York, though born near Knaresborough, he was arrested for handing the priest John Boste a mug of ale. He was also charged with treasonable words. Acquitted at trial, he was moved by Judge Rhodes from the city gaol to the Castle and tried a second time on the same charge at the Lammas Assizes.

One offence counted against him was a remark made as the priest Francis Ingleby was dragged on a hurdle to execution. Hearing a minister's wife call Ingleby a traitorly thief, Bickerdike answered that he was no thief, but as true as she was. Those words were held to be the cause of his death. Condemned at the second trial, he suffered at York on 5 August, or by another account 8 October, 1585.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-dymoke:
Robert Dymoke was a Lincolnshire gentleman who died a confessor of the faith in Lincoln gaol in 1580. Son of Sir Edward Dymoke of Scrivelsby, hereditary King's Champion, he received the martyr priest Richard Kirkman at his house in 1579 and kept him as schoolmaster to his sons. At the time Dymoke only occasionally conformed to the state religion, but he was reconciled in 1580, by Kirkman or by Edmund Campion.

In July 1580 he and Bridget, his wife and daughter of the Earl of Lincoln, were charged with hearing Mass and recusancy. Though helpless with paralysis, Dymoke was carried to gaol on the order of the Bishop of Lincoln. There he died faithful to the end. In his last hours Protestant ministers tormented him, trying to turn him, and would not leave him in peace even when half unconscious. His eldest son Edward was already over twenty-one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salt-lake:
Salt Lake names a diocese covering Utah and more than half of Nevada, a vast western see drawn with surveyor's care. Utah alone spans 350 miles north to south and nearly 300 at its widest, with 84,970 square miles in all, of which 2,780 are water. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia maps the diocese county by county across desert and mountain.

From Nevada the diocese takes Elko, Lander, Eureka, White Pine, Lincoln, and Nye, some 71,578 square miles in the eastern part of that state. Its western edge starts at the Oregon line two miles west of the 117th meridian, runs south a hundred miles to the Battle Mountains, then turns sharply. The entry gives bishops, parishes, and the hard conditions of Catholic life in Mormon country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sampson-erdes:
Sampson Erdeswicke, Staffordshire antiquarian, died in 1603 after a life spent as a Catholic gentleman under penal laws. Born at Sandon, son of Hugh Erdeswicke, descended from Richard de Vernon of the Conqueror's reign, he entered Brasenose College, Oxford, as a gentleman-commoner in 1553. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a scholar shaped by his father's sufferings.

Hugh, named to the Privy Council in 1582 by the Anglican bishop of Coventry as the sorest and most dangerous papist in England, lost much for the faith. Sampson, back in Staffordshire under Catholic bans, poured himself into a thorough Survey of Staffordshire, the work by which he is known. Not printed while he lived, its manuscript history stays tangled, and the entry sorts the editions that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sherbrooke:
Sherbrooke, a diocese in Quebec suffragan to Montreal, was erected by Pius IX on 28 August 1874 from parts of Three Rivers, Saint Hyacinthe, and Quebec. It covers the Eastern Townships, famed for fertile soil, industry, and commerce, and now counts 74 parishes. The first missionaries came early in the 1800s, among them Jean Raymbault, John Holmes, Michael Power, Hugh Paisley, and Hubert Robson. The last three died tending fever-stricken Irish in 1847.

From 1834 to 1874 many missionaries labored among a Catholic population thinly scattered over an immense tract. Roads were often unknown, and they traveled on horseback or on foot through dense forests infested with wolves and bears. The first bishop was Antoine Racine, ordained in 1844 and consecrated in 1874, who ruled nineteen years. The entry closes with schools, an old folks home, an orphans home, and a hospital second to none in Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-burke:
Thomas Burke, Bishop of Ossory, was born at Dublin about 1709 and died at Kilkenny in 1776. Sent to Rome in 1723, he joined the Dominicans before his fifteenth birthday and proved a gifted student, rising through the order's schools to become regent of studies for six years. In 1742 the master general conferred on him the degree of Master of Theology.

Returning to Dublin in 1743, he took up parish ministry, and in 1753 he was named historian of his province. In 1759 he became Bishop of Ossory, a see he governed for seventeen years. He is best remembered for Hibernia Dominicana, published in 1762 after four years of labour, with a Supplementum added in 1772 defending the papal nuncio Rinuccini.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-nichol:
Thomas Nicholas Burke, a celebrated Dominican orator, was born at Galway in 1830 and died at Tallaght, Ireland, in 1882. A bout of typhoid at fourteen and the famine year of 1847 turned his thoughts to religion, and late that year he asked to join the Dominicans. He made his novitiate at Perugia, studied in Rome, and served while still a student as novice-master at Woodchester.

Ordained priest in March 1853, he returned to Ireland in 1855 to found the Irish novitiate at Tallaght. His 1859 sermon on church music made him famous overnight, and he became prior of Tallaght in 1863. Later he preached across Ireland, England and America, drawing crowds with a voice and presence that made him the best known Irish preacher of his day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-willia:
Thomas William Croke, Archbishop of Cashel, was born near Mallow, County Cork, in 1824 and died at Thurles in 1902. He studied at the Irish College in Paris and finished his theology at Rome. Back in Ireland he taught at St. Patrick's College, Carlow, then worked at Charleville through the famine years, when suffering deepened his national feeling.

A follower of O'Connell and later of Young Ireland, he became president of St. Coleman's College, Fermoy, in 1858, pastor of Doneraile, and then Bishop of Auckland, New Zealand. He took part in the closing sessions of the Vatican Council. In 1874 he returned as Archbishop of Cashel, where his fellow countrymen saw him as the ideal patriot priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ulick-joseph-:
Ulick Joseph Bourke was an Irish scholar and writer born at Castlebar, County Mayo, on 29 December 1829. He died there on 22 November 1887. Son of Ulick Bourke and Cecilia Sheridan, he was cousin to Archbishop MacHale of Tuam. He learned Irish at a Castlebar academy and then at Errew Monastery under the historian James Hardiman. He entered St Jarlath's College, Tuam, in 1846, and Maynooth in 1849. He was ordained priest in 1858.

Bourke taught Irish, logic, and humanities at St Jarlath's, and his books carried Irish learning to a wide readership. His College Irish Grammar and Easy Lessons stayed standard handbooks of modern Irish. His lives of MacHale, his plea for Mayo's evicted tenants, and his unfinished Irish dictionary show a scholar joined to public causes. The entry lists his works and notes that, though some theories are now out of date, his English works still open Irish philology and archaeology to newcomers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-mo:
William of Moerbeke was a thirteenth-century Flemish Dominican whose Greek-to-Latin translations carried Aristotle to the Latin West. Born about 1215, he died in 1286. He kept company with Aquinas, Campanus, Witelo, and Henri Bate, and lived at the papal court of Viterbo in 1268. He attended Lyons in 1274, and held the See of Corinth from 1277 until his death.

At Aquinas's request he translated Aristotle whole or revised older versions, becoming the first translator of the Politics about 1260. His versions are word-for-word and faithful, plain rather than elegant, yet prized as classics by the fourteenth century. Beyond Aristotle he rendered Hero, Archimedes, Simplicius, and Proclus, whose Theological Elements, dated Viterbo 18 May 1268, with the Book of Causes, fed the century's Neo-Platonic current. Witelo and Bate both dedicated works to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-pike:
William Pike was a Dorset joiner martyred at Dorchester in December 1591 for holding to Rome. Living at West Moors, West Parley, he met the martyr Thomas Pilchard on the road from Dorchester and was converted, probably in 1586. At trial for reconciliation with Rome, judges pressed the bloody question of papal supremacy, and Pike frankly upheld Rome's authority, earning a traitor's death sentence. Pleas to recant for his family's sake met a bold refusal.

Pike answered that it ill became a son of Pilchard to give way, and Pilchard's name stayed on his lips until he died. Asked at the end what had moved him to his resolve, he quipped that nothing had but the smell of a pilchard, a pun on his converter's name. His exact death date is unrecorded, but the Menology lists him under 22 December, and his story stands in Pollen's Acts of the English Martyrs.
christian-s-mistake:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, author of John Halifax, Gentleman, opens her novel half an hour after a wedding at Avonsbridge. Christian Oakley, only child of a late esquire, has married Dr. Arnold Grey. He is master of Saint Bede's College, about forty-five, spare and iron-grey. She is twenty-five years younger, graceful, pale, and unnaturally composed. A silversmith's wife is already drafting the Times notice.

The age gap and a second marriage set the terms. Grey counts the cost of everything before he acts. Christian must learn a household ruled by that habit. A child called Titia, creeping in and out of her father's house and lying about it, tests Christian's gentleness mid-book. She promises no hardness for the truth told. The mistake of the title works itself out slowly, in domestic weather.
doe-osti-17026347-wdh-dataset-ai-readine:
Curator intake form, version 1.0, gives reviewers a standard way to judge whether a data set earns an AI ready label. Bridget Thrasher, Chitra Sivaraman, and Michael Kieburtz are the named authors. The form splits judgment into two readings: whether machines can find, load, parse, and legally reuse the data, and whether the documentation explains it well.

Each item gets one of five verdicts, from Met down to Not assessed, with evidence noted beside it. Any essential item left partial, unmet, or unresolved blocks the label. Passing data sets climb three tiers, Baseline, Mature, and Reference, as more items are met. Sections cover file standards, site and time metadata, quality flags, and limits on reuse.
doe-osti-3020472-close-out-project-descr:
Mark E. Koepke's close-out report for DOE grant DE-SC0021405, a West Virginia University plasma physics project that began September 1, 2020, is an unusually candid ending. The project, titled 'Decomposing Turbulence: Nonmodal vs. Modal Approach,' set out to document signatures of non-modal behavior in plasma turbulence tied to flow shear. The close-out states directly that this objective was not achieved.

The experiments aimed at an electromagnetic shear-driven instability in the Large Area Plasma Device, working at plasma beta between 0.001 and 0.3, far above earlier experiments. The team tried to launch or trigger Alfven waves in the shear layer between coaxial plasmas. Koepke and collaborators at the Naval Research Laboratory and elsewhere ran the design, data collection, and interpretation. The report records the parameters reached and the personnel involved, leaving a clear account of what was attempted.
doe-osti-3376722-seismic-velocity-modeli:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-25375, issued June 30, 2026, by Ellen Syracuse, refines the seismic map under the Nevada National Security Site, with a close look at Rock Valley. How fast quake waves move through each rock layer is the key to placing a quake. The team ran a joint inversion, one solve fitting the speed map and fresh spots for past quakes. Better spots sharpen safety work and test monitoring at the site.

Frenchman Flat gets a full read. There, slow compression waves, under 5.5 kilometers per second, reach four kilometers deep. Shear waves top 3.0 kilometers per second as shallow as half a kilometer. That split hints the depth rule used for old rock at Rock Valley may not fit here. The slow zone is read as thick volcanic rock from the Miocene, over older stone. Little Skull Mountain shows the same slow cap to four kilometers.
doe-osti-3377646-marine-fuel-innovation-:
National Laboratory of the Rockies slides from January 2026 lay out an analysis of new marine fuels for ports on the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway. The printed team is Kelcie Kraft, Veronika Semchukova, Kristen Lu, and Emily Newes. The work was done with Great Lakes ports for the Department of Energy's Office of International Affairs and the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation.

The deck reviews fuel production capacity in the region, the land that fuel plants would need, and port infrastructure. Proposed plants could add about 1.5 million tons of marine diesel oil equivalent per year by 2031. Tables also size solar power for ports such as Duluth-Superior, Chicago, and Detroit, and the team demonstrates the APEX tool for port planning.
ethelyn-s-mistake:
Mary J. Holmes, writing as Mrs. Mary J. Holmes, fills the title page with a long list of her earlier novels, and Ethelyn's Mistake stands among them in her uniform series. The contents set out the shape of the story at once: Ethelyn, the Van Buren set, Richard Markham, a bridal, and a honeymoon. Marriage to Richard brings Ethelyn into his mother's household at Olney, where Mrs. Markham's ways soon press hard on the young wife.

Later chapters move through Washington visits, days of waiting, a crisis, and letters, until the husband is left deserted and an investigation follows. Holmes lingers on household detail: soda biscuits made below stairs, relatives like Aunt Barbara in Chicopee, and small rulings that shape a marriage. Readers get a domestic novel of pride, patience, and a union tested over years before its final accounting.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-luke:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on St. Luke begins with the births that open the Gospel. Alexander Maclaren labels this first volume as Luke chapters I to XII. Elijah Come Again treats John the Baptist's promise. The Magnificat and Zacharias's Hymn follow in chapter I.

Shepherds and Angels and Simeon's Swan-Song come from chapter II. The Boy in the Temple closes the childhood section. Later entries include The Temptation and Preaching at Nazareth. A Sabbath in Capernaum and Laws of the Kingdom show his range. The Two Debtors and Love and Forgiveness draw on chapter VII. Maclaren preaches Luke as the Gospel of mercy and prayer.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewmanSamMike_N:
An FBI memorandum dated November 25, 1963 concerns Sam Mike Newman of New Orleans. Newman owned the property at 544 Camp Street. Agents reported on Cubans seen there, in company with associates of Guy Banister. Banister, a former FBI man turned private investigator, ran his office at that address.

544 Camp Street became one of the most examined addresses in the case. Oswald had stamped it on leaflets he handed out for a pro-Castro group. A memo written three days after the assassination shows agents already working the building's tenants and visitors. Newman's name enters the record as landlord, a small part in a building that would not leave the story.
govdocs-archive_org-politica-aeterna-ale: Aleksandr Dugin's Politica Aeterna treats politics as metaphysics. Its subtitle names the two poles of the book: political Platonism and what Dugin calls the Black Enlightenment. The work belongs to his Noomachia: Wars of the Mind series. Dugin, a Russian philosopher, builds a system in which ideas and myths fight for the future. The volume presents that system at length for readers of his political philosophy.
govdocs-archive_org-the-history-of-etrur: The History of Etruria, Volume 1: the volume - the declassified government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated material, filed. An obscure item, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the literature and readers.
hassan-the-story-of-hassan-of-bagdad-and:
James Elroy Flecker, an English poet and diplomat, set his play Hassan in Baghdad of the Arabian Nights. Hassan, a confectioner of forty-five, boils sugar in his sweetshop and dreams of elsewhere. His friend Selim teases the longings out of him in the scene. Flecker builds the play in five acts of song-filled verse.

The Caliph Haroun ar Raschid walks the city with his minstrel Ishak, vizier Jafar, and executioner Masrur. Rafi, King of the Beggars, and the girl Yasmin cross Hassan's path as court and street collide. Pervaneh, Hassan's love, grounds his dreaming in shop and home. Gifts from the Caliph turn to terror as Hassan sees how power amuses itself with pain. At last he quits Baghdad on the golden journey to Samarkand. Flecker's play, staged after his death, became known for its caravan finale and its warning that beauty and cruelty share one throne.
joe-s-luck-or-always-wide-awake:
Joe's Luck, or Always Wide Awake, is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger Jr., printed in a 1913 New York edition. Alger wrote many such tales, including Tony the Tramp, The Cash Boy, and Do and Dare. Chapter one introduces Joe, a stout boy of fifteen with an honest, sun-browned face. He works as a servant in the Norton household.

The book opens with a small act of defiance. Oscar Norton orders Joe to brush him off, and Joe flatly refuses. He says he will not be ordered round, though Oscar calls it impudence and asks if he has turned lazy. Joe's firm stand sets the pattern for Alger's hero: poor, proud, and awake to every chance.
kindness-to-animals-or-the-sin-of-cruelt:
Kindness to Animals is Charlotte Elizabeth's book for children, issued by the American Sunday-School Union at Philadelphia. It was entered according to Congress's act in 1845. The first chapter explains the plan: this is not natural history. Elizabeth tells only of animals she has known and watched herself since childhood.

Nothing appears in the book, she promises, that is not exactly true so far as she knows. Watching animals kept her mind busy in early life, and she commends the habit to children. Incidents from her own animals carry the lessons in kindness. Elizabeth, a popular religious writer, taught mercy to dumb creatures as a Christian duty. Her little book belongs to the Sunday-school shelf of improving tales for the young.
krindlesyke:
Wilfrid Wilson Gibson published Krindlesyke with Macmillan in London in 1922. It is a long dramatic poem in two books. Gibson notes that an early draft of Book One appeared in 1910.

He rewrote that first book completely for this edition. Book Two, written from 1919 to 1922, had not been printed before. Gibson says the work was not planned for the stage. He flavors the speech with local northern words, mostly words of feeling that readers can grasp from context. North country speech and farm life ground the poem's drama. Gibson lets plain voices carry grief, love, and stubborn pride.
may-brooke:
Anna Hanson Dorsey wrote May Brooke, held in rights by P. J. Kenedy in 1888. The book also bears the name Conscience, or, The Trials of May Brooke. Uncle Stillinghast and May herself lead the first two chapters.

A morning errand, Aunt Mabel, and tales of past and present follow. Troubled waters, trials, and a warning test the young heroine. A midnight messenger, a new will, and a secret sin deepen the plot. Repentance appears twice in the heads, and remorse stands near the end. Helen gets a chapter of her own amid the trials. Faith and conscience steer the plot more than wealth or rank.
mike:
P. G. Wodehouse published Mike, a public school story, in London in 1909. Its hero, Mike Jackson, arrives at school already famous for cricket. The frontispiece quotes a fan asking about his batting average of fifty-one. Twelve full-page illustrations by T. M. R. Whitwell accompany the text.

Early chapters cover the journey down, the nets, and a row with the town. Mike finds friends, scrapes, and a great picnic in his first terms. Wodehouse writes about Wrykyn school life with affection and comic timing. The novel began his long series of school and cricket stories, and introduced readers to his lightest manner.
miss-merivale-s-mistake:
Mrs. Henry Clarke opens this novel with a startling discovery. Miss Merivale, tired from the long drive from Woodcote, half-dozes while two girls talk at the window. A name, Rhoda Sampson, makes her sit bolt upright with anxious curiosity. The frontispiece shows Pauline Smythe studying a photograph frame.

Pauline's diplomacy and suspicions drive much of the plot. Tom and Rhoda meet, invitations are issued, and a confession follows. A visit to Kentish Town and the figure of Polly Smith deepen the mystery of identities. Clarke writes a Victorian tale of mistaken names, family secrets, and an older woman's error.
my-lady-nicotine-a-study-in-smoke:
J. M. Barrie wrote these light essays on smoking, his lady Nicotine. M. B. Prendergast drew the pictures for the Boston edition. Chapter one compares matrimony and smoking, to comic effect. My first cigar and the Arcadia mixture follow.

Barrie writes of his pipes, pouch, and smoking table with mock care. Friends like Gilray, Marriot, and Jimmy fill the middle chapters. A houseboat named Arcadia hosts more smoke and talk. The romance of a pipe cleaner gets its own tale. Barrie turns a small habit into bright, whimsical prose, years before Peter Pan made him most famous.
never-fail-blake:
Arthur Stringer wrote Never-Fail Blake, a mystery issued in New York with a 1913 copyright by the Bobbs-Merrill Company. The book was sold under the banner Supertales of Modern Mystery. Its frontispiece shows a suitor asking, then why can't you marry me?

Blake serves as a second deputy, and the tale opens in his office. A woman named Elsie walks in, silk rustling, and sits at the end of his desk. Blake greets her without looking up, in a gloomy, hound eyed mood. Old ties between the two hang over the talk. Crime, office work, and a past romance drive Stringer's story from there.
on-a-torn-away-world-or-the-captives-of-:
Roy Rockwood wrote this boys' adventure in the Great Marvel series. Other series titles promise trips to both poles and Mars. The contents open with a chapter called Shot Into the Air. Mark hangs on in the second chapter's title. A great earthquake tears the heroes' world apart.

Courage and quick thinking help the young heroes survive. Rockwood wrote fast, fantastic tales for young readers. The book belongs with early science adventure for boys. Peril follows peril in a strange, broken landscape. It is pure thrill fiction of its period.
podcast-dannyjones-bq3Y0qE7AKE:
Brigham Buhler joins Danny Jones to argue that doctors are barred by law from telling patients the full truth. The episode title calls him a pharma whistleblower. Buhler speaks from his work in health care and his break with the drug trade.

Buhler claims drug firms hide cures and punish doctors who step out of line. He names the rules and fears that keep doctors quiet, as he sees them. Jones asks which claims rest on paper he can show. Listeners get a sharp charge against the drug trade from a man who worked in it. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-dannyjones-vD0y4xUxnKE:
Diane Hennacy joins Danny Jones to tell how she saw a test that should not be possible. The episode title bills her as a Harvard doctor. Her tale centers on a mind test with results that broke the rules she knew.

Hennacy tells the tale in full, from the setup of the test to the score that stunned the room. She talks about what the result did to her view of the mind. Jones asks what checks were run to rule out tricks. Listeners get a quiet, strange story told by a trained mind. The library holds the talk as an archive record of her account.
podcast-joerogan-2DGXoLiwLkE:
Dr. Shanna Swan joins Joe Rogan for episode 1638 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Swan is an epidemiologist who studies how chemicals in daily goods harm fertility. Her book warned of a steep fall in sperm counts in the West.

Swan lays out her finds on plastics, sprays, and the parts of the body they bend. She argues the harm starts in the womb and builds for life. Rogan asks what a man can cut from his home now. Listeners get a grave health talk with steps they can take. The library keeps the episode as a record of her stated work.
podcast-joerogan-KoM8f5Gp3kE:
Psychedelic research pioneer Amanda Feilding joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2002. Feilding founded the Beckley Foundation and spent decades funding studies the mainstream would not touch, from LSD brain scans to cannabis policy. Few people have done more to restart the field.

She tells Rogan how she began, what the early scans showed, and where she wants the research to go next. Rogan asks about her famous self-experiments and the cost of working outside the academy. The episode is a rare long hearing with the woman many scientists credit for psychedelic science's return.
podcast-tuckercarlson-_QV7WpLaHkE:
Veteran Braxton McCoy joins Tucker Carlson to talk Iraq, opioids, and defending American land. McCoy was wounded in Iraq, then fought opioid addiction after coming home. He later became a voice for keeping US land out of foreign and corporate hands.

McCoy tells his war story and the harder battle with pain pills that followed. He explains how foreign governments and giant firms are buying farmland and why he resists it. Carlson connects the fights into one veteran's triple battle, abroad and at home. Patriots and the concerned get a plain, hard-earned perspective.
poems-of-william-blake:
William Blake's poems appear here in his two great song cycles, the Songs of Innocence and of Experience, together with the Book of Thel. Blake etched and printed these books himself in the late eighteenth century, selling a handful of copies while London ignored him. The Innocence songs open with a piper commanded by a laughing child on a cloud to pipe a song about a lamb. Then to write his happy songs in a book every child may read.

The Shepherd follows, praising the sweet lot of a life spent praising among the sheep. Experience answers Innocence poem by poem, with the same world seen through loss, anger, and knowledge. Thel, a young spirit hesitating before birth and experience, closes the volume in dialogue with the small creatures of her vale. No short book in English holds more per page.
selections-from-the-speeches-and-writing:
Edmund Burke's speeches and writings fill this chosen volume, fronted by a long opening essay on his life and rank. The essay places Burke high in what it calls the aristocracy of mind. It records his birth at Dublin in 1730, his attorney father, and his boyhood schooling in the country.

Burke entered Trinity College and rose to fame as a speaker of rare force and moral weight. The essay quotes Quintilian on the orator as a good man, whose words carry a judge's trust. Readers get both Burke's own pages and a portrait of the statesman whom later ages kept honoring.
seneca-naturales-quaestiones-clarke:
John Clarke translated Seneca's Naturales Quaestiones in 1910 as Physical Science in the Time of Nero. Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and Nero's adviser, wrote the work around 62 CE. It is the Roman encyclopedia of natural phenomena.

Lightning, earthquakes, comets, rainbows, and the Nile's floods all receive books. Seneca asks how nature works and how a wise person should meet it. He gathers Greek science into Latin with moral reflections attached. Comets, then feared as omens, get a calm and rational treatment. Clarke's translation keeps the Stoic's curiosity bright for English readers. The work shows Roman science at its most inquiring before Seneca's forced death.
sonnets-and-sonnets-on-english-dramatic-: Algernon Charles Swinburne's Sonnets and his Sonnets on English Dramatic Poets (1590-1650) are taken from Volume V of his Collected Poetical Works. The 1917 Heinemann issue at London notes a first printing by Chatto in 1904, with reprints through 1912. The opening list of sonnets names Hope and Fear, After Sunset, and A Study from Memory, then sonnets to Dr. John Brown and to William Bell Scott, and A Death on Easter Day.
tales-of-the-chesapeake:
Geo. Alfred Townsend, who signed his work Gath, published Tales of the Chesapeake in New York in 1880. Townsend gave the book to his father and noted that his kin had first come to Chesapeake Bay in 1623 and settled on the Pocomoke River.

Townsend says two pieces, Kidnapped and Dominion over the Fish, had run in Chambers's Journal in London. A poem, Herman of Bohemia Manor, is new, and all the pieces share one bay region. Readers get verse and prose steeped in oyster fleets, old houses, and local lore, from a writer who knew the shore as home ground.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-42-luk:
Luke , read in the King James Version, begins with a writer's preface. Many, he says, have taken in hand to set out in order a declaration of things most surely believed among them.

Those accounts were delivered by eyewitnesses and ministers of the word from the beginning. It seemed good to Luke also, with perfect understanding from the first, to write in order to Theophilus. His aim is certainty about what Theophilus was taught. The narrative then turns to Herod's days and a priest named Zacharias, whose wife Elisabeth was of the daughters of Aaron.
the-collected-poems-of-rupert-brooke:
Rupert Brooke's collected poems appear here in a 1915 edition, with an introduction by George Edward Woodberry and a biographical note by Margaret Lavington. A short life record heads the book. Brooke was born at Rugby on August 3, 1887, and became a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge, in 1913.

He took a commission as a sub-lieutenant in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve in September 1914 and joined the Antwerp expedition that October. He sailed with the British Mediterranean Expeditionary Force on February 28, 1915, and died in the Aegean on April 23, 1915. Woodberry's introduction dwells on his vivid life. Brooke was fair to see and winning in his ways, Woodberry writes, and above all there was life in him. His senses met the world with surprise and delight, tasting each thing as if it were a fresh discovery. Lavington's note and poems about Brooke close the volume.
the-god-of-his-fathers-tales-of-the-klon:
The God of His Fathers: Tales of the Klondyke gathers short tales. They first ran in magazines such as McClure's, Ainslee's, and Outing. This edition is from Sir Isaac Pitman and Sons, dated 1906. The contents list eleven tales. They run from the title story through Siwash and The Man with the Gash. They name Grit of Women and A Daughter of the Aurora.

The title tale opens on the primeval forest. The old struggle for life still rages there. Briton and Russian overlap in the Land of the Rainbow's End. Yankee gold has not yet bought the land. Wolf packs pull down caribou. Native peoples live under chiefs and medicine men. They drive out bad spirits and fight their neighbors. Into that harsh world the tale brings white men and their faiths.
the-high-school-boys-training-hike:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Boys' Training Hike, subtitled Making Themselves Hard as Nails. Chapter titles include The Deed of a Hero, The Peddler and the Lawyer's Half, The No-Breakfast Plan, Making the Tramps Squirm, and Dick Prescott, Knight Errant. Chapter one opens with Dick Prescott trying to hire a wagon from Mr. Newbegin Titmouse.

Dick offers ten dollars, and Titmouse asks if that means per week. Dick answers no: ten dollars for the whole month of August. Titmouse cries that the sum is absurd for the use of a fine wagon. The haggling sets a comic tone for a hike built around rough travel, peddlers, tramps, and hard training.
the-lady-of-the-lake:
Sir Walter Scott's poem appears here in a Boston school edition of 1883. William J. Rolfe edited it with notes. He had been head master of the High School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. His preface explains his work. He borrowed cuts from an illustrated edition. A cheaper annotated one was his aim. Then he found the text itself troublesome. No two editions agreed exactly. Even Black's Author's Edition was full of misprints.

He compared the first edition of 1810 line by line. A London bookseller supplied it. The Edinburgh edition of 1821 and a dozen others joined the check. He restored first-edition readings where later changes were not Scott's. His examples are precise. Clift had corrupted to cliff, heat to heart. Boune became bound, barded became barbed. The volume serves students reading Scott's Highland romance. Ellen Douglas and the disguised king fill it.
the-lake:
George Moore's novel appears here in a 1921 William Heinemann edition. Its opening pages carry his dedicatory letter in French. Édouard Dujardin is its addressee. The date is August 17, 1905. Moore confesses a theft in it. Busy correcting proofs in Paris, he stole a title. Dujardin's work in progress, La Source du Fleuve Chrétien, supplied it. A character in Moore's novel bears the stolen name. Ralph Elles never appears but is much talked of. The dedication compensates the larceny.

The letter drifts into memory. Decades of talk about literature and music lie behind them. His Confessions of a Young Englishman appeared in Dujardin's Revue Indépendante. Hours at Fontainebleau and Valvins return to him. No orchestra is needed to explain his poor country's sadness, Moore writes. A single flute on an island in a lake suffices. The epistle sets the key for an Irish priest's story.
the-philosopher-s-joke:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote The Philosopher's Joke, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company. The narrator opens by saying he does not believe the story himself. Six persons are persuaded of its truth, and their hope is to convince themselves it was an hallucination. Their trouble is that there are six of them, close friends who cannot get away from one another.

The man who told it, called Armitage, though that is not his real name, confessed it one night in a club smoking room. He hoped the narrator's flippant scepticism would show him the absurd side. Jerome frames a strange tale as a secret its witnesses long to disbelieve, and the narrator promptly, discreetly, tells Mrs. Armitage, who bursts into tears.
the-poems-of-henry-van-dyke: The Poems of Henry Van Dyke is shown here in a new and revised edition with many hitherto uncollected pieces. Arthur F. Bird published it at London in 1925. Here only the title page and a list of the author's books appear, so the poems themselves are absent. That list names prose volumes Little Rivers and Out-of-Doors in the Holy Land. It names story collections The Blue Flower and The Unknown Quantity. Poem volumes such as The White Bees appear too, along with the play The House of Rimmon.
the-songs-of-a-sentimental-bloke:
C. J. Dennis wrote these Australian verse tales of the Sentimental Bloke, a working-class larrikin in love, and a foreword by a fellow writer introduces them warmly. The foreword recalls how the poems, running in the Bulletin, brightened dark days, and calls the Bloke more perfect than any earlier larrikin character, the writer's own beloved Benno included.

Readers meet a man longing to be something better, and Doreen, the girl he courts, whom the foreword praises as standing for all good women. Dennis's slang-filled humour, the foreword warns, can hide the tenderness underneath, so the introduction asks readers to notice both the jokes and the feeling.
the-tempting-of-tavernake:
E. Phillips Oppenheim begins The Tempting of Tavernake on the roof of a grim London boarding-house near Russell Square. A young American girl leans against the railing, staring over the housetops with a gloomy, rebellious expression. Tavernake, uncompromisingly English, has followed her up through the trap-door and stands watching her in silence. They are almost strangers, bound only by boarding-house etiquette and a few greetings.

vegetius-de-re-militari-clarke:
Vegetius composed De Re Militari, the Military Institutions of the Romans, around 390 CE. John Clarke's English translation appeared in 1767. Vegetius boiled centuries of Roman practice into a handbook for emperors.

Recruiting, training, marching, and siegecraft receive orderly, practical treatment. He laments that the army of his day had let old discipline slip. His famous line says that wanting peace means preparing for war. Medieval generals prized the book above all other military writing. Kings and commanders consulted it for a thousand years after Rome fell. Clarke's version keeps the old reformer's bluntness in plain English.

The story opens in the days of King Herod with a priest named Zechariah. His wife Elizabeth, old and childless, is of Aaron's line. While Zechariah burns incense in the temple, an angel appears at the altar. Fear grips him at the sight. Weymouth's neat prose fits Luke's careful, linked style of telling.
